children.title: What Is the Internet?
children.summary: Introduces the Internet from a nuts-and-bolts view (end systems, communication links, packet switches, ISPs), a services view supporting distributed applications, and defines what a protocol is and why all Internet communication is governed by protocols.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the Internet from both a nuts-and-bolts view (end systems, links, packet switches, ISPs) and a services view supporting distributed applications.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners often conflate the Internet with the World Wide Web, when the Web is only one of many distributed applications the Internet supports.
Learners may believe Internet applications run inside packet switches in the network core, when in fact they run only on end systems.
Learners may think of the Internet as one monolithic network rather than a network of networks interconnected through a hierarchy of ISPs.
Learners may assume only traditional computers connect to the Internet, overlooking things like thermostats, watches, game consoles, and cars.

children.title: The Network Edge
children.summary: Covers end systems (hosts) and how they connect to the network: access networks such as DSL, cable, FTTH, Ethernet, WiFi, and cellular, plus guided and unguided physical media (twisted pair, coax, fiber, radio).

children.title: End Systems and Their Role
children.summary: What hosts (end systems) are, where they sit at the network edge, and their role in running network applications before connecting to the network core.
children.learning_objective: The learner can define end systems (hosts), give examples of them, and explain that they sit at the network edge where they run network application programs.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often think end systems are only desktop computers, when they also include servers, mobile devices, and non-traditional 'things' attached to the Internet.
Students may believe hosts are located throughout the network core, when they actually sit at the edge of the Internet.
Students may think network applications run inside the network or on ISPs, when application programs actually run on the end systems themselves.
Students may confuse end systems with ISPs or packet switches, when end systems are the devices that access the Internet through ISPs.

children.title: Home Access: DSL, Cable, and FTTH
children.summary: Wired residential access technologies: DSL over telephone lines, cable over HFC (shared vs. dedicated bandwidth), and fiber to the home, including typical data rates.
children.learning_objective: The learner can compare DSL, cable (HFC), and FTTH home access technologies in terms of their underlying infrastructure, typical data rates, and shared versus dedicated bandwidth.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners often believe DSL and cable both provide dedicated bandwidth, when in fact DSL offers dedicated access to the CO while cable users share the HFC downstream and upstream channels with their neighborhood.
Learners may think FTTH always shares a single fiber among homes, not realizing there are competing distribution architectures such as direct fiber, AONs, and PONs.
Learners frequently confuse the roles of the DSLAM in DSL networks and the CMTS at the cable head end, which perform the analogous function of separating/terminating many home connections.
Learners often assume upstream and downstream rates are equal, overlooking that DSL and cable are typically asymmetric with lower upstream rates.

children.title: Ethernet and WiFi Access
children.summary: Local access via Ethernet LANs in homes and enterprises, and IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs in homes, offices, and public hotspots.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe how end devices obtain local Internet access through Ethernet LANs (via twisted pair and Ethernet switches) and through 802.11 wireless LANs via access points connected to the wired Internet, including typical access rates.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing a WiFi access point connects directly to the Internet rather than to a wired network (typically Ethernet) that in turn connects to the wired Internet.
Assuming wireless LAN access delivers the same access rates as wired Ethernet, when Ethernet users typically have 100 Mbps to tens of Gbps to the switch.
Thinking Ethernet LAN access requires fiber or coaxial cable, when it typically uses twisted-pair copper wire (e.g., category 6a reaching 10 Gbps up to 100 meters) to connect to an Ethernet switch.

children.title: Cellular and Wide-Area Wireless Access
children.summary: Mobile access through cellular networks (3G, LTE/4G, 5G), enabling untethered Internet access for hand-held devices over wide areas.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe how cellular networks (4G LTE and 5G) provide wide-area untethered Internet access to mobile hand-held devices and identify the key architectural elements involved.

common_misconceptions.description: Cellular networks are often mistakenly thought of as telephony-only systems, when modern 4G/5G networks provide both voice and high-speed Internet access.

Learners may assume cellular network architecture is fundamentally different from the Internet, when in fact 4G networks adopt Internet principles like protocol layering, edge/core separation, and separation of data and control planes.
Learners often conflate WiFi and cellular access, not realizing they are distinct wireless access technologies with different coverage areas and architectures.
Learners may assume cellular links offer the same performance as wired links, ignoring that the shared wireless spectrum makes bandwidth a scarce resource for applications.

children.title: Guided Physical Media
children.summary: Characteristics and uses of guided media: twisted pair (UTP/STP), coaxial cable, and optical fiber, including where each is deployed.
children.learning_objective: The learner can identify the main guided physical media (twisted pair, coaxial cable, optical fiber) and describe the characteristics and deployment scenarios of each.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing fiber-optic technology completely replaced twisted pair, when in fact modern twisted pair (e.g., category 6a achieving 10 Gbps up to 100 meters) remains the dominant solution for high-speed LAN networking.
Assuming twisted pair is used only inside LANs, when it is also commonly used for residential Internet access via dial-up modem and DSL technologies.
Thinking the physical medium must be of the same type for every transmitter-receiver pair along a source-to-destination path, when in fact the medium can vary along the route.
Classifying terrestrial or satellite radio spectrum as guided media, when guided media refers to solid physical media like copper wire, coaxial cable, and fiber, while radio spectrum is unguided.

children.title: Unguided Physical Media
children.summary: Wireless propagation of signals in radio channels: terrestrial microwave, WiFi/cellular radio bands, and satellite links, and how the environment affects them.
children.learning_objective: The learner can identify the categories of physical media and describe unguided (wireless) media such as terrestrial radio spectrum and satellite radio spectrum, recognizing that signals propagate as electromagnetic waves without a physical conductor.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners often assume the physical medium must be of the same type for every transmitter-receiver pair along a path, when in fact different media can be used along the same route.
Learners may think wireless transmission has no physical medium at all, when it actually uses the radio spectrum (a shared physical medium) through which electromagnetic waves propagate.
Learners may assume unguided media behave identically to guided media like twisted pair or fiber, ignoring that the shared, open radio spectrum makes propagation subject to environmental effects.

children.title: The Network Core
children.summary: Examines the mesh of links and packet switches at the Internet's core: store-and-forward packet switching and statistical multiplexing, circuit switching with FDM/TDM, and the Internet's structure as a network of networks of ISPs.

children.title: Store-and-Forward Packet Switching
children.summary: How packet switches receive, store, and retransmit packets; per-hop transmission delay and computing the end-to-end delay of a message crossing N links and N-1 switches.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how packet switches receive, store, and retransmit packets using store-and-forward transmission and compute the end-to-end delay of a message crossing N links and N-1 switches.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners often attribute store-and-forward delay to processing or queueing at the switch, when it actually comes from each switch having to fully receive (transmit in) the packet before it can begin transmitting it on the next link.
Learners may believe a packet is transmitted on all links of the path simultaneously, rather than hop-by-hop where each switch must store the full packet before retransmitting it.
Learners may compute end-to-end delay using only one link's transmission time, forgetting that each of the N links adds a full per-hop transmission delay (L/R).
Learners may think switches store and forward the entire message, when in fact the source breaks the message into smaller packets that are forwarded individually.

children.title: Queuing Delay, Packet Loss, and Statistical Multiplexing
children.summary: Output buffers in packet switches, queuing delay when packets arrive faster than the output link can transmit, packet loss under congestion, and how statistical multiplexing shares link capacity on demand.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how queuing delay arises at a router's output buffer, how it varies with traffic intensity, and why finite queue capacity causes packet loss under statistical multiplexing.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that queuing delay grows without bound as traffic intensity approaches 1, when in reality finite queue capacity means packets are dropped instead of waiting indefinitely.
Assuming a lost packet results from corrupted bits, when from the network's perspective loss typically occurs because a packet arrives to find a full router queue and is dropped.
Thinking that larger router buffers always improve performance, ignoring that bigger buffers can add queuing delay that harms interactive applications and slows TCP's response to congestion.

children.title: Circuit Switching with FDM and TDM
children.summary: Dedicated end-to-end circuits with reserved bandwidth, circuit setup and teardown, and how frequency-division and time-division multiplexing partition a link among active circuits.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how FDM and TDM partition a link's bandwidth among dedicated circuits and compute a circuit's transmission rate and total file-transfer time, including circuit setup overhead.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing each TDM circuit transmits at the full link rate rather than at the frame rate times the bits per slot (i.e., the link rate divided among the slots).
Assuming that bandwidth reserved for an idle circuit can be used by other circuits, when in fact circuit switching wastes capacity during silent periods.
Forgetting to include end-to-end circuit establishment time when calculating how long it takes to send data over a circuit-switched network.
Thinking FDM and TDM yield different per-circuit capacities on the same link, when both give each circuit an equal dedicated fraction of the link's bandwidth.

children.title: Packet Switching vs. Circuit Switching
children.summary: Trade-offs between the two core approaches: efficiency for bursty traffic, wasted capacity during silent periods, guaranteed versus on-demand bandwidth, and why the Internet adopts packet switching.
children.learning_objective: The learner can compare circuit switching and packet switching in terms of resource reservation, efficiency for bursty traffic, and user capacity, and explain why the Internet adopts packet switching.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often believe circuit switching delivers lower delay for all traffic patterns, overlooking the connection-setup time and the reserved capacity that sits unused during silent periods.
Students may think packet switching avoids delay entirely, but when more users are simultaneously active than the link's capacity allows, output queues grow and packets must wait.

Students may assume both approaches support the same number of users on a link, when statistical multiplexing actually lets packet switching serve roughly three times as many bursty users with comparable performance.
Students may believe packet switching reserves resources like circuit switching does, when it actually uses buffers and transmission rates on demand with no reservation.

children.title: The Internet as a Network of Networks
children.summary: How access ISPs (home, mobile, enterprise) interconnect through regional ISPs, national and global tier-1 providers, peering, IXPs, and content provider networks to form today's Internet structure.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe how the Internet is structured as a network of networks, in which access ISPs are interconnected through higher-tier ISPs and content-provider networks so that all end systems can exchange packets.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing the Internet is one single large network rather than a hierarchy of interconnected networks owned and operated by different providers.

Assuming each access ISP directly connects to every other access ISP, when in reality interconnection is achieved through regional, national, and global tier-1 providers and content-provider networks.
Thinking the Internet's structure evolved purely for performance reasons, when much of its evolution was driven by economics and national policy.
Assuming content providers like Google merely connect to the Internet as customers, rather than operating their own private global TCP/IP networks that interconnect their data centers.

children.title: Delay, Loss, and Throughput
children.summary: Builds quantitative models for packet-switched networks: processing, queuing, transmission, and propagation delays; queuing delay and packet loss; end-to-end delay; and throughput including the bottleneck-link model.

children.title: Sources of Nodal Delay
children.summary: Introduces the four delay components at a node—processing (dproc), queuing (dqueue), transmission (dtrans), and propagation (dprop)—and the nodal delay formula dnodal = dproc + dqueue + dtrans + dprop. Compares the relative magnitude of each component across link types (e.g., negligible propagation on a campus LAN vs. hundreds of milliseconds over a geostationary satellite link; negligible transmission delay at 10 Mbps vs. significant on dial-up).
children.learning_objective: The learner can identify the four components of nodal delay (dproc, dqueue, dtrans, dprop), combine them into the formula dnodal = dproc + dqueue + dtrans + dprop, and compare the relative magnitude of each component across link types such as campus LANs, satellite links, and dial-up modems.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners often conflate propagation delay (time for signal to travel over the medium, dependent on distance) with transmission delay (time to push packet bits onto the link, dependent on link rate and packet size).

Learners may assume each delay component has a fixed typical value, when in fact a single component can range from negligible (microseconds of propagation on a campus LAN) to significant (hundreds of milliseconds over a geostationary satellite link).

Learners may believe that increasing link bandwidth reduces propagation delay, when bandwidth only affects transmission delay, which is why dtrans is negligible at 10 Mbps but hundreds of milliseconds on dial-up links.
Learners may assume that because processing delay is typically negligible (microseconds or less), it is irrelevant, overlooking that it strongly influences a router's maximum forwarding throughput.

children.title: Queuing Delay and Traffic Intensity
children.summary: Examines the most complex delay component: queuing delay. Covers how it depends on the traffic intensity La/R, including behavior as intensity approaches 0 (negligible delay), approaches 1 (delay grows large and highly variable), and exceeds 1 (average queue length unbounded). Notes the impact of queuing delay variation (jitter) on applications.
children.learning_objective: The learner can compute the traffic intensity La/R for a link and predict the resulting queuing delay behavior as the intensity approaches 0 (negligible), approaches 1 (large and highly variable), or exceeds 1 (queue grows without bound).

common_misconceptions.description: Students often think La/R > 1 merely causes longer delays, when in fact the average queue grows without bound and the queuing delay approaches infinity (with finite buffers, packets are instead dropped).
Students may believe a traffic intensity of exactly 1 is a stable operating point, when in practice delay becomes large and highly variable as the intensity approaches 1.
Students may assume La/R exactly characterizes queuing delay statistics, when for realistic random arrivals it only provides an intuitive estimate of the extent of the delay.
Students may treat queuing delay like a constant per-packet delay such as transmission delay, when it actually varies from packet to packet depending on the queue state.

children.title: Packet Loss
children.summary: Explains that router queues have finite capacity, so a packet arriving to find a full queue is dropped (lost). Relates loss to traffic intensity approaching or exceeding 1, and describes how, from an end-system viewpoint, a lost packet appears as one that never arrives rather than one with infinite delay.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain why a router drops a packet when its finite queue is full and describe how such loss appears from an end-system viewpoint, relating loss to traffic intensity approaching or exceeding 1.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often think that as traffic intensity approaches 1, packet delays approach infinity, when in reality finite queues cause arriving packets to be dropped (lost) instead.
Students may believe an end system can distinguish a lost packet from a heavily delayed one, whereas from the end-system viewpoint a lost packet simply looks like one that never arrives.
Students may assume that increasing router buffer capacity always improves performance, overlooking that larger buffers can introduce much longer queueing delays.

children.title: End-to-End Delay
children.summary: Defines end-to-end delay as the accumulation of nodal delays (plus other delays) along the source-to-destination path. Includes application-induced delays such as the packetization delay in Voice-over-IP, where the sender must fill a packet with encoded digitized speech before transmission, affecting user-perceived call quality.
children.learning_objective: The learner can compute end-to-end delay as the accumulation of nodal delays (processing, queuing, transmission, propagation) along the source-to-destination path and identify application-induced components such as VoIP packetization delay.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners think end-to-end delay equals the nodal delay at a single router rather than the sum of nodal delays accumulated across all routers on the path.
Learners believe end-to-end delay consists only of the four nodal delay components, overlooking application-induced delays such as the packetization delay in Voice-over-IP.

Learners assume each delay component contributes equally on every link, when in fact contributions vary significantly, e.g., negligible campus-link propagation versus hundreds of milliseconds over a geostationary satellite link.
Learners attribute VoIP packetization delay to routers or links rather than to the sending application's need to fill a packet with encoded digitized speech before transmission.

children.title: Throughput and the Bottleneck Link
children.summary: Defines instantaneous and average end-to-end throughput for a file transfer, and presents the bottleneck-link model: throughput equals the minimum transmission rate along the path, min{Rs, Rc}. Uses this to approximate file transfer time as F/min{Rs, Rc} (e.g., a 32 Mbit MP3 over a 1 Mbps bottleneck takes 32 seconds) and notes these are approximations ignoring store-and-forward and processing delays.
children.learning_objective: The learner can compute end-to-end throughput as the minimum transmission rate along the path (the bottleneck link, min{Rs, Rc}) and estimate file transfer time as F/min{Rs, Rc}.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing end-to-end throughput is the sum or average of the link rates along the path rather than the minimum transmission rate.
Assuming the fastest link (e.g., a high-rate server) determines transfer speed, when in fact the slowest (bottleneck) link limits throughput.
Treating F/min{Rs, Rc} as an exact transfer time, ignoring that it is an approximation that omits store-and-forward delays, processing delays, and protocol issues.
Assuming throughput depends only on the transmission rates of the links on the path, when shared links and intervening traffic can further reduce it.

children.title: Protocol Layers and Service Models
children.summary: Explains why networks use a layered architecture, the service each layer provides, the five-layer Internet protocol stack, and how messages are encapsulated layer-by-layer as they traverse the sender's and receiver's stacks.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain the advantages of protocol layering and identify the five layers of the Internet protocol stack together with the service each layer provides.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing each layer resides in a single dedicated device, when in fact a layer n protocol is distributed as pieces across end systems, packet switches, and other network components.
Confusing changing the implementation of a service with changing the service itself, not realizing a layer can change how it implements its function without affecting other layers.
Assuming layering is universally beneficial, overlooking that one layer may duplicate lower-layer functionality and that some researchers and engineers oppose layering.
Confusing the five-layer Internet protocol stack (physical, link, network, transport, application) with other layered models that have a different number of layers.

children.title: Networks Under Attack
children.summary: Surveys prevalent Internet security attacks, including malware (viruses and worms), denial-of-service attacks, packet sniffing, and IP spoofing, motivating the study of network security.
children.learning_objective: The learner can identify and describe the prevalent classes of Internet security attacks—malware (viruses and worms), denial-of-service and distributed denial-of-service attacks, packet sniffing, and IP/source masquerading—and explain why networks need to be secured against them.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often conflate a single-source DoS attack with a distributed DoS (DDoS) attack, not realizing that DDoS attacks use many controlled sources (e.g., botnets) and are therefore much harder to detect and defend against.

Students may think an attacker must send all the crippling traffic themselves at rate R from one machine, overlooking that in a DDoS the aggregate rate across all controlled sources only needs to be approximately R.
Students may believe security is a separate discipline unrelated to core networking, when in fact attacks like sniffing and spoofing directly exploit how the Internet and its protocols work.
Students may lump all attacks together as 'hacking', failing to distinguish the distinct classes of malware, denial of service, sniffing, source masquerading, and message modification/deletion.

children.title: History of Computer Networking
children.summary: Traces the development of packet switching and the evolution of computer networking and the Internet from its early research origins to today's Internet.
children.learning_objective: The learner can trace the major milestones in the history of computer networking, from the independent invention of packet switching through ARPAnet and the Cerf-Kahn internetworking work to the separation of IP from TCP.

common_misconceptions.description: Packet switching was invented by a single research group, when in fact three groups around the world independently developed it, unaware of each other's work.
TCP and IP were always separate protocols, when early versions of TCP combined reliable in-sequence delivery with forwarding functions before IP was split out and UDP was developed.

The Internet grew from a single network, when it actually emerged from multiple separate networks (ARPAnet, Cyclades, SNA, time-sharing networks) that required an encompassing internetworking architecture.

children.title: Principles of Network Applications
children.summary: Network application architectures (client-server vs. P2P), processes communicating through sockets, transport services available to applications, transport services provided by the Internet (TCP vs. UDP), and what an application-layer protocol defines.

children.title: Network Application Architectures
children.summary: Contrast client-server architectures (data centers, always-on servers) with P2P architectures (self-scalability, minimal server infrastructure) and hybrid designs, including examples like Web, e-mail, and file sharing.
children.learning_objective: The learner can distinguish client-server, peer-to-peer (P2P), and hybrid application architectures and identify which paradigm a given application (e.g., Web, e-mail, file sharing) uses.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often conflate the application architecture with the network architecture, even though the network architecture is fixed and the application architecture is chosen by the application developer.
Learners may believe P2P architectures eliminate servers entirely, when in practice minimal server infrastructure is still typically required.
Students may assume a 'server' in a client-server architecture is always a single physical machine rather than a data center of always-on hosts.
Learners may think the choice between client-server and P2P is imposed by the underlying network rather than being a design decision made by the application developer.

children.title: Processes Communicating
children.summary: Explain how processes on different end systems communicate: client vs. server processes, the socket as the interface between an application process and the transport layer, and addressing a destination process via IP address and port number.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how processes on different end systems communicate by exchanging messages through a socket (the software interface between the process and the transport layer) and identify the roles of client and server processes.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that processes on different hosts communicate directly with each other, when in fact they communicate by exchanging messages across the underlying network.
Confusing a socket with a physical hardware component, when it is actually a software interface through which a process sends messages into and receives messages from the network.
Assuming that communication between processes on the same host (governed by the operating system) works the same way as communication between processes on different end systems across a network.
Thinking that client and server refer to types of machines, rather than to the roles of processes, where the client initiates the connection and the server is the process contacted.

children.title: Transport Services Available to Applications
children.summary: Identify the four classes of service an application may need from a transport layer: reliable data transfer, throughput guarantees, timing guarantees, and security.
children.learning_objective: The learner can identify the four classes of service an application may need from a transport-layer protocol: reliable data transfer, throughput guarantees, timing guarantees, and security.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing every application requires all four transport services, when in fact different applications match different subsets of services to their needs.
Confusing elastic applications (e.g., email, file transfer, Web) with bandwidth-sensitive ones, since elastic apps can use as much or as little throughput as happens to be available.
Conflating throughput guarantees with timing guarantees, which are two distinct dimensions of transport service.
Assuming an application developer can request arbitrary services, when in practice one must choose among the services offered by available transport protocols such as UDP and TCP.

children.title: Transport Services Provided by the Internet
children.summary: Describe the TCP service model (connection-oriented, reliable, congestion control) versus the UDP service model (connectionless, unreliable, minimal), and note why neither provides throughput, timing, or security guarantees (motivating SSL/TLS).
children.learning_objective: The learner can identify the two transport protocols the Internet offers (TCP and UDP) and explain how to select between them based on the services they provide to applications.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing the Internet provides many transport-layer protocol choices, when in fact it makes only two available to applications: UDP and TCP.
Assuming the choice between UDP and TCP is arbitrary or purely preferential, rather than a deliberate matching of protocol services (e.g., reliability, throughput, timing) to the application's needs.
Assuming that any transport service an application might desire (like guaranteed throughput or timing) is provided by the Internet, when the available protocols only offer a limited set of services.
Failing to recognize that possible transport-layer services can be broadly classified along four dimensions (reliable data transfer, throughput, timing, and security) when comparing protocols.

children.title: Application-Layer Protocols
children.summary: Define what an application-layer protocol specifies—message types, message syntax, field semantics, and rules for when/how processes send and respond to messages—and distinguish open protocols (e.g., HTTP, SMTP) from proprietary ones.
children.learning_objective: The learner can define what an application-layer protocol specifies—message types, message syntax, field semantics, and rules for when and how processes send and respond to messages—and distinguish open protocols like HTTP and SMTP from proprietary ones.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing an application-layer protocol only defines the syntax of messages, when it also specifies message types, the semantics of fields, and the rules for when and how processes send and respond to messages.
Assuming an application-layer protocol governs communication within a single machine, when it actually defines how processes running on different end systems exchange messages.
Assuming all application-layer protocols are open standards like HTTP and SMTP, when some application-layer protocols are proprietary.

children.title: The Web and HTTP
children.summary: Overview of HTTP, non-persistent vs. persistent connections, HTTP message format, user-server interaction with cookies, web caching, and HTTP/2.

children.title: Overview of HTTP
children.summary: Web page structure (HTML base file plus referenced objects), URLs, browsers and Web servers as HTTP client/server, and HTTP's stateless request-response model.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe HTTP as the Web's application-layer protocol, explaining its client-server request-response model and its stateless nature.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing HTTP is the entire Web application, when it is only one component (the application-layer protocol) alongside browsers and Web servers.
Assuming HTTP keeps track of clients between requests, when in fact HTTP is a stateless protocol that retains no information about clients.
Thinking a Web server may be intermittently available, when in the client-server architecture a Web server is always on with a fixed IP address.
Confusing the roles of request and response messages, not realizing the client sends the HTTP request and the server retrieves the object and encapsulates it in an HTTP response.

children.title: Non-Persistent vs. Persistent Connections
children.summary: How HTTP uses TCP connections: non-persistent connections with one object per connection, persistent connections with multiple objects, and response-time analysis using round-trip time.
children.learning_objective: The learner can distinguish non-persistent from persistent HTTP connections and compute response times for downloading objects using round-trip time.

common_misconceptions.description: Students may believe a single non-persistent HTTP connection can carry multiple objects, when in fact each object requires its own separate TCP connection with handshaking.
Students often assume fetching an object takes only one round-trip time, overlooking that non-persistent HTTP needs two RTTs per object (TCP setup plus request/response) plus transmission time.
Students may think persistent connections eliminate all waiting time, when they only eliminate the TCP connection-establishment RTT since each object still needs a request/response RTT.
Students may assume parallel instances of non-persistent HTTP always speed up downloads, ignoring that N parallel connections each receive only 1/N of the link bandwidth.

children.title: HTTP Message Format
children.summary: Structure of HTTP request messages (request line, header lines, methods like GET and POST) and response messages (status line, status codes, headers, entity body).
children.learning_objective: The learner can identify the structure of HTTP request messages (request line with method, URL, and version fields plus header lines) and response messages (status line, header lines, and entity body) and explain the purpose of their key fields.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing the Host header line is unnecessary because the TCP connection already identifies the server, when in fact it is required by Web proxy caches.
Thinking the request line contains only the URL, when it actually has three fields: the method, the URL, and the HTTP version.
Confusing the sections of a response message by treating the entity body as part of the status line rather than as a separate section containing the requested object.
Assuming status codes like 400 Bad Request and 404 Not Found indicate server failures, when they signal problems with the client's request.

children.title: User-Server Interaction: Cookies
children.summary: The four cookie components (cookie file, header lines, backend database) and how cookies enable stateful user identification over a stateless protocol.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the four components of cookie technology and trace how Set-cookie and cookie header lines, the browser-managed cookie file, and the back-end database work together to identify users across sessions over stateless HTTP.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often believe the cookie file is stored at the Web server, when it is actually kept on the user's end system and managed by the user's browser.
Students may think cookies make HTTP itself a stateful protocol, when in fact HTTP remains stateless and cookies merely create a user-session layer on top of it.

Students may assume the cookie value alone identifies the user, when identification depends on the server's back-end database associating the cookie's identification number with user-specific information.
Students may think cookies are used only for shopping carts or e-commerce, when any site wishing to restrict access or serve content as a function of user identity can use them.

children.title: Web Caching
children.summary: Proxy servers as caches, cache hits and misses, benefits of caching (reduced response time and traffic), and the conditional GET for keeping cached copies fresh.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how a Web cache (proxy server) satisfies HTTP requests via cache hits and misses, describe the benefits of caching in reducing response time and traffic, and outline how the conditional GET keeps cached copies up to date.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often think a Web cache is only a server or only a client, when in fact it acts as a server to browsers and as a client to the origin server.

Students may believe a conditional GET always results in the server sending the full object, when in fact the server sends the object only if it has been modified since the cached copy's last-modified date.
Students may think improving response time always requires upgrading the access link, overlooking that installing an inexpensive Web cache can achieve lower response times without a link upgrade.
Students may conflate Web caching of HTTP objects with DNS caching of hostname-to-IP mappings, which are distinct mechanisms in different application-layer services.

children.title: HTTP/2
children.summary: HTTP/2's framing mechanism, multiplexing of requests/responses over one TCP connection, and how it addresses head-of-line blocking and improves page-load latency.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how HTTP/2's framing mechanism multiplexes request and response messages over a single TCP connection to reduce head-of-line blocking and improve page-load latency.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often think HTTP/2 changes HTTP methods, status codes, URLs, or header fields, when in fact it only changes how data is formatted and transported.
Students may believe that reducing to a single TCP connection would hurt performance, not realizing it enables multiplexing and lets TCP congestion control operate as intended.
Students may think framing fully eliminates head-of-line blocking, when it is designed only to reduce or mitigate HOL blocking at the application/message level.
Students may assume the client must explicitly request every object, not knowing HTTP/2 allows the server to push additional objects for a single request.

children.title: Electronic Mail in the Internet
children.summary: SMTP for mail transfer, mail message formats (headers and body), and mail access protocols used to retrieve messages.

children.title: E-mail System Architecture
children.summary: The three main components—user agents, mail servers, and the SMTP protocol—plus mailboxes, message queues, and how a message flows from sender to recipient's mailbox, including failure handling and retries.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the three principal components of the e-mail system (user agents, mail servers, and SMTP) and trace how a message flows from the sender's user agent through mail servers, mailboxes, and outgoing message queues to the recipient's mailbox.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing the sender's user agent delivers messages directly to the recipient's mail server, when in fact the message is first placed in the sender's mail server and relayed from there.
Confusing the recipient's mailbox, which stores received messages until retrieval, with the outgoing message queue, which holds messages awaiting delivery by the sender's mail server.
Assuming SMTP is used to read or fetch mail from a mailbox, when SMTP is a transfer/relay protocol and retrieval is handled by mail access protocols such as IMAP or HTTP.
Thinking an e-mail travels in one hop from sender to receiver, rather than as a multi-step relay between user agents and mail servers.

children.title: SMTP: Mail Transfer Protocol
children.summary: How SMTP (RFC 5321) transfers messages between mail servers: client/server roles, TCP port 25, direct delivery, command/reply dialogue, and its restrictions and differences from HTTP.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how SMTP (RFC 5321) transfers messages between mail servers, including client/server roles, TCP port 25, direct delivery, and its restrictions and differences from HTTP.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often think a failed delivery places the message on an intermediate mail server, when in fact it stays in the sender's mail server queue and is retried later.
Students may assume SMTP works like HTTP for continuous content transfer, overlooking that SMTP is an older legacy protocol with restrictions such as limiting message bodies to simple 7-bit ASCII.
Students may believe the sender's user agent delivers mail directly to the recipient's mail server, when typically it relays through the sender's own mail server acting as an SMTP client.
Students may think a mail server is exclusively a client or a server, when in fact it acts as an SMTP client when sending and an SMTP server when receiving mail.

children.title: Mail Message Formats and MIME
children.summary: The structure of an e-mail message with header lines (From:, To:, Subject:, Received:) and body, and MIME extensions that allow multimedia content in the body.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the structure of an e-mail message—RFC 5322 header lines (From:, To:, Subject:, Received:) separated from the body by a blank line—and explain how MIME extends the message format to carry multimedia content in the body.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners may think the header lines are part of the message body, rather than a separate section defined by RFC 5322 that is separated from the body by a blank line (CRLF).
Learners may conflate the From: header line inside the mail message with the SMTP MAIL FROM: command used during message transfer, treating them as the same thing.
Learners may think MIME is a separate transfer protocol, rather than an extension to the mail message format that allows multimedia content to be included in the body.
Learners may assume header lines are machine-encoded fields, when in fact each header line is readable text consisting of a keyword followed by a value.

children.title: Mail Access Protocols: POP3, IMAP, and HTTP
children.summary: How recipients retrieve messages from their mail server: POP3 (download-and-delete vs. download-and-keep), IMAP (folders and server-side manipulation), and web-based e-mail over HTTP.
children.learning_objective: The learner can compare the POP3, IMAP, and HTTP-based mail access protocols and explain how each is used to retrieve messages from a recipient's mail server.

common_misconceptions.description: The learner believes POP3 always deletes messages from the server after download, overlooking its download-and-keep mode.
The learner thinks IMAP merely downloads messages like POP3 rather than allowing users to organize folders and manipulate messages directly on the server.
The learner believes HTTP is only for browsing web pages and cannot be used for e-mail, when web-based e-mail services retrieve messages over HTTP.
The learner assumes SMTP is used to fetch mail from the server, confusing the message-transfer protocol with the recipient-side access protocols.

children.title: DNS: The Internet's Directory Service
children.summary: Services provided by DNS and an overview of how DNS works, including its distributed, hierarchical name-server structure.

children.title: Services Provided by DNS
children.summary: Why a directory service is needed (hostnames vs. IP addresses), DNS's main task of translating hostnames to IP addresses, host aliasing with canonical names, and load distribution via DNS rotation among replicated servers.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the services DNS provides to Internet applications—translating hostnames to IP addresses, supporting host aliasing, and distributing load among replicated servers via DNS rotation.

common_misconceptions.description: DNS is an application that users directly interact with, like the Web or e-mail, rather than a core service invoked by other applications and software.
DNS's sole function is hostname-to-IP-address translation, ignoring its additional services such as host aliasing and load distribution.
When a DNS server returns a set of IP addresses for an alias, the ordering of addresses is fixed, rather than rotated in each reply to spread traffic across replicated servers.
DNS itself forwards client traffic to replicated servers, when in fact distribution happens because clients typically send their HTTP request to the first IP address listed in the rotated reply.

children.title: DNS Server Hierarchy: Root, TLD, and Authoritative
children.summary: DNS as a distributed database in a hierarchy of servers running BIND over UDP port 53; the roles of root servers (13 root servers, 1000+ instances), top-level-domain servers, and authoritative servers.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the three classes of DNS servers in the hierarchy (root, TLD, and authoritative) and explain the sequence of steps in resolving a hostname through them.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often think there are only 13 root servers, when in fact there are 13 distinct root server identities with over 1000 instances worldwide.
Students may believe the local DNS server is part of the DNS server hierarchy, when it is actually outside the hierarchy though central to the architecture.
Students may think the root server directly returns the IP address of the requested hostname, when it actually returns TLD server addresses, delegating down the hierarchy.
Students may conflate authoritative servers with the local/default name server provided by an ISP, though they play different roles in resolution.

children.title: DNS Query Resolution: Recursive and Iterative
children.summary: How a hostname lookup proceeds: the local DNS server's role, delegation from root to TLD to authoritative servers, intermediate servers in the chain, and the difference between recursive and iterative queries.
children.learning_objective: The learner can trace a DNS hostname lookup from the local DNS server through root, TLD, and authoritative servers and distinguish recursive from iterative queries.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing the root DNS server returns the final IP address, when it actually returns a referral to TLD servers responsible for the suffix.
Thinking that a chain of queries issued by the local DNS server is recursive, when in iterative resolution the local server itself sends each successive query.
Assuming the local DNS server is authoritative for the queried hostname, when it acts only as an intermediary forwarding queries on the host's behalf.
Believing the requesting host contacts root, TLD, and authoritative servers directly, rather than delegating the resolution to its local DNS server.

children.title: Exploring DNS with dig
children.summary: Hands-on use of the dig tool to trace the delegation chain of DNS queries from a root server down to authoritative servers for real websites.
children.learning_objective: The learner can use the dig tool to initiate queries starting from a root DNS server and trace the delegation chain of DNS servers down to the authoritative server for real websites.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing dig only returns the final IP address of a hostname, rather than revealing the intermediate DNS servers in the delegation chain.
Thinking the root DNS server directly returns the IP address of the queried hostname instead of delegating the query to TLD and authoritative servers.
Assuming every DNS query traverses the full root-to-authoritative chain, ignoring that caching often allows the local DNS server to bypass root and TLD servers.
Thinking dig queries root servers directly, when in practice the local DNS server forwards queries along the hierarchy.

children.title: Peer-to-Peer File Distribution
children.summary: How P2P architectures distribute a file among peers and how this scales compared with client-server distribution.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how P2P file distribution enlists peers to redistribute file data and compare how its minimum distribution time scales with the number of peers versus the client-server architecture.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that in P2P distribution the server must still send a full copy of the file to every peer, when in fact peers redistribute received portions to other peers on the server's behalf.

Assuming P2P distribution time grows linearly and without bound with the number of peers just like client-server, when in fact P2P distribution time is self-scaling and remains bounded (e.g., under F/u in the textbook example).
Confusing distribution time with the time for one peer to download the file, when it is defined as the time until all N peers have obtained a copy.
Thinking P2P is always faster independent of peer capabilities, when the analysis depends on peer upload rates and assumes bottlenecks lie in the access networks rather than the Internet core.

children.title: Video Streaming
children.summary: How streaming applications deliver stored video over the Internet, including the bandwidth and timing considerations unique to streaming media.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how stored video is streamed over the Internet, including the role of average end-to-end throughput, video compression at multiple bit rates, and how DASH adapts chunk selection to available bandwidth.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often assume bandwidth is constant during streaming, overlooking that mobile users' available bandwidth fluctuates as they move relative to base stations.
Students may think the server decides which video version to send, when in DASH the client itself measures received bandwidth and runs the rate-determination algorithm to select each chunk.

Students may believe any network connection can stream video smoothly, not realizing that continuous playout requires average end-to-end throughput at least as large as the compressed video's bit rate, otherwise freezing delays occur.

Students may view multiple compressed versions purely as a quality trade-off, missing that creating versions at different bit rates (e.g., 300 kbps, 1 Mbps, 3 Mbps) is precisely what enables adaptation to varying client bandwidths.

children.title: Socket Programming with TCP and UDP
children.summary: The socket interface and development of simple client-server network applications in Python, over both TCP and UDP.

children.title: Simple Client-Server Application Example
children.summary: The running example used for both protocols: the client reads a line from the keyboard and sends it, the server converts the characters to uppercase and sends them back, and the client displays the modified line. Also covers the requirement that the server be up and running before the client sends its message.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the flow of the simple client-server application in which the client sends a keyboard-entered line, the server converts it to uppercase and returns it, and the client displays the modified line, including the requirement that the server be running before the client sends its message.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing the client can send its message before the server program is up and running, when in fact the server must be running as a process before the client sends its message.
Thinking the server performs complex processing, when in the example it simply converts the received characters to uppercase and sends them back.
Assuming the modified line returned by the server is not shown to the user, when the client displays the modified line after receiving it.

children.title: Socket Programming with UDP
children.summary: Connectionless programming with UDPClient.py and UDPServer.py: creating a datagram socket, sending independent packets with sendto()/recvfrom(), destination address attached to each packet, and the OS automatically attaching the source IP address and port number. No handshake or delivery guarantees.
children.learning_objective: The learner can write and trace a Python UDP client-server pair (UDPClient.py/UDPServer.py) that creates a datagram socket and exchanges packets using sendto()/recvfrom() with the destination address attached to each packet.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that, as with TCP, a UDP client must first establish a connection with the server before sending data.
Thinking the application code must explicitly attach its own source IP address and port number to each packet, when in fact the operating system does this automatically.
Assuming UDP provides delivery guarantees or a reliable byte stream like TCP, when it actually sends independent packets with no such guarantees.
Assuming the destination address is fixed at socket creation, rather than being supplied with each packet via sendto().

children.title: Socket Programming with TCP
children.summary: Connection-oriented programming with TCPClient.py and TCPServer.py: handshaking to establish a TCP connection before data flows, the client socket and server socket, the distinction between the welcome socket and the connection socket, and the reliable byte-stream channel between the two end systems.
children.learning_objective: The learner can write and run a simple TCP client-server application (TCPClient.py and TCPServer.py), correctly distinguishing the welcome socket from the connection socket and explaining the handshaking and reliable byte-stream behavior of the TCP connection.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners often think the server uses a single socket for all clients, not realizing that a separate connection socket is created for each client after the welcome socket accepts initial contact.
Learners may assume, as with UDP, that the sender must attach a destination address to each piece of data, when in TCP the connection is established once and data is simply dropped into the socket.
Learners may believe the handshake is part of data exchange, rather than a preliminary step that must complete before the client and server can send data to each other.
Learners may conflate TCP's reliable, in-order byte-stream service with UDP's connectionless, no-guarantee delivery when deciding which transport to use.

children.title: Comparing TCP and UDP Socket Programs
children.summary: Side-by-side comparison of the two program pairs: connection setup versus connectionless operation, byte-stream versus independent datagrams, number and role of sockets on each side, and how addressing is handled, to understand when each API is appropriate.
children.learning_objective: The learner can compare TCP and UDP client-server socket programs by contrasting connection setup versus connectionless operation, byte-stream versus independent datagrams, and the number and role of sockets on each side, and select the appropriate API for a given application.

common_misconceptions.description: TCP is always preferable to UDP because its reliable data transfer makes it the right choice for every application, ignoring UDP's advantages such as finer application-level control over what data is sent and when.
A TCP server uses just one socket for all clients, just like a UDP server, rather than needing a welcoming socket plus a separate connection socket for each client.
UDP socket programs, like TCP programs, must establish a connection before any data can be exchanged between client and server.
TCP and UDP deliver data to the receiving application in the same way, overlooking that TCP provides a reliable byte-stream channel while UDP sends independent packets with no delivery guarantees.

children.title: Choosing a Transport Protocol and Port Numbers
children.summary: The first development decision: whether the application runs over TCP (connection-oriented, reliable byte stream) or UDP (connectionless, no delivery guarantees). Also covers using well-known port numbers when implementing an RFC-defined protocol and avoiding them when developing a proprietary application.
children.learning_objective: The learner can choose between TCP and UDP for a new application by comparing the services each transport protocol offers, and assign an appropriate port number, using well-known ports for RFC-defined protocols and avoiding them for new proprietary applications.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often assume TCP is always the correct choice because it is reliable, overlooking applications whose needs are better matched by UDP's no-frills, connectionless service.
Students may believe any port number can be freely chosen for any application, when in fact RFC-defined protocols must use their standardized well-known port numbers (e.g., HTTP on 80, FTP on 21).
Students may think a port number identifies a host on the network, when it actually identifies a specific socket/process on a host so the transport layer can demultiplex arriving segments.
Students may assume the transport protocol is selected automatically at runtime, when it is actually an explicit design decision made by the application developer when creating sockets.

children.title: Introduction and Transport-Layer Services
children.summary: Logical end-to-end communication between application processes on different hosts; the relationship between the transport and network layers and how the underlying network service model constrains transport services; overview of the Internet's transport protocols (UDP and TCP).
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how the transport layer provides logical end-to-end communication between application processes on different hosts, and describe how the network layer's service model constrains the transport services (such as reliable data transfer, throughput, timing, and security) offered by UDP and TCP.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that the transport and network layers provide the same service, when in fact the network layer delivers between hosts while the transport layer extends this to logical communication between application processes.

Thinking that logical communication means the hosts are physically directly connected, when in reality they may be on opposite sides of the planet connected through numerous routers and a wide range of link types.
Assuming TCP is the only Internet transport protocol, overlooking that UDP is the other transport-layer protocol examined in this chapter.

Assuming an application can demand any combination of transport services, when in practice an application must pick among the available protocols whose service offerings may be constrained by the underlying network.

children.title: Multiplexing and Demultiplexing
children.summary: How the transport layer delivers segments to the correct application sockets using port numbers; connectionless (UDP) demultiplexing based on two-tuples versus connection-oriented (TCP) demultiplexing based on four-tuples.
children.learning_objective: The learner can define transport-layer multiplexing and demultiplexing and explain how a receiving host uses segment header fields to deliver data to the correct socket.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that the network layer's host-to-host delivery already gets data to the application, when in fact multiplexing/demultiplexing is needed to extend delivery to the process-to-process level.
Thinking the transport layer delivers segments directly to application processes, when it actually directs them to the process's socket.

Confusing the two directions, e.g., assuming demultiplexing happens at the sender, when demultiplexing is the receiving job and multiplexing is the gathering of data chunks from sockets at the source host.
Assuming multiplexing and demultiplexing are unique to Internet transport protocols, when they arise at any layer where a single lower-layer protocol serves multiple higher-layer protocols.

children.title: Connectionless Transport: UDP
children.summary: UDP's minimal, no-frills service model, why applications choose it, its segment structure (header fields), and how the UDP checksum is computed and used for error detection.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain UDP's minimal connectionless service model, identify the fields of a UDP segment including the checksum, and describe why applications choose UDP despite its lack of delivery guarantees and congestion control.

common_misconceptions.description: UDP provides reliable, in-order delivery guarantees similar to TCP because it is a transport-layer protocol.
UDP establishes a connection with the receiver before exchanging data, like TCP does.
UDP performs no processing at all and simply passes application messages straight through to the network layer.
The UDP checksum can repair corrupted segments rather than only detecting errors.

children.title: Principles of Reliable Data Transfer
children.summary: Building a reliable channel over an unreliable network layer: ARQ with acknowledgments and retransmissions, sequence numbers, stop-and-wait versus pipelined operation, and the Go-Back-N (GBN) and Selective Repeat (SR) protocols.

children.title: Reliable Transfer over a Perfectly Reliable Channel (rdt1.0)
children.summary: The baseline case where the underlying channel never corrupts or loses packets; the sender and receiver FSMs need no feedback, sequence numbers, or retransmissions. Serves as the starting point for incrementally adding reliability mechanisms.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the sender and receiver FSMs of rdt1.0 and explain why a perfectly reliable channel requires no feedback, sequence numbers, or retransmission mechanisms.

common_misconceptions.description: Students may think the receiver must send acknowledgments back to the sender, although with a perfectly reliable channel nothing can go wrong and no feedback is needed.
Students may assume rdt1.0 uses sequence numbers, ACKs, or retransmissions like later rdt versions, when in fact it employs none of these mechanisms.
Students may believe rdt1.0 would work over real lossy or bit-corrupting channels rather than only under the perfect-channel assumption.
Students may assume the packet carries control fields or differs from the raw data unit, although in rdt1.0 there is no difference between a unit of data and a packet.

children.title: Reliable Transfer over a Channel with Bit Errors (rdt2.x)
children.summary: Introduces ARQ mechanisms: checksums for error detection, ACKs/NAKs, and retransmission on negative feedback. Covers handling corrupted ACKs/NAKs by adding sequence numbers (rdt2.1) and eliminating NAKs by ACKing the last correctly received packet (rdt2.2).
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how ARQ protocols (rdt2.x) achieve reliable transfer over a channel with bit errors using checksums, ACKs/NAKs, retransmissions, sequence numbers, and NAK-free duplicate ACKs.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often believe an explicit NAK message is required for negative feedback, when in fact rdt2.2 replaces NAKs by ACKing the last correctly received packet.
Students may think duplicate ACKs signal a lost ACK rather than indicating to the sender that the packet following the ACKed one was not correctly received.
Students may assume the basic stop-and-wait protocol of rdt2.0 suffices once ACKs are added, not realizing that corrupted ACKs/NAKs require sequence numbers (rdt2.1) to detect ambiguity.
Students may believe ACK messages need not carry the sequence number of the acknowledged packet, whereas rdt2.2 requires ACK, 0 or ACK, 1 in the acknowledgment.

children.title: Reliable Transfer over a Lossy Channel (rdt3.0)
children.summary: Handles lost packets and premature timeouts using a countdown timer and retransmission, with sequence numbers letting the receiver detect and discard duplicates. Shows why alternating-bit sequence numbers suffice for stop-and-wait operation.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how rdt3.0 achieves reliable data transfer over a lossy channel by combining a countdown timer, retransmission on premature timeouts, and alternating-bit sequence numbers that let the receiver detect and discard duplicate packets.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners often think that a retransmitted packet after a timeout is delivered to the application a second time, overlooking that sequence numbers let the receiver detect and discard duplicates.
Learners may believe a lost acknowledgment means the original data was lost, when rdt3.0 simply retransmits the packet and the receiver handles the resulting duplicate.
Learners may view the countdown timer as a performance optimization rather than the essential mechanism that detects lost packets and triggers retransmission.
Learners may assume reliable transfer over a lossy channel requires a large sequence-number space, when alternating 0/1 values suffice for stop-and-wait operation.

children.title: Stop-and-Wait Performance and Channel Utilization
children.summary: Quantifies how stop-and-wait wastes bandwidth (e.g., only 267 kbps effective throughput on a 1 Gbps link) and derives utilization as a function of RTT and L/R, motivating the shift to pipelined operation.
children.learning_objective: The learner can compute the sender utilization and effective throughput of a stop-and-wait protocol from RTT, packet size L, and link rate R, and explain why pipelined operation is needed to overcome this limitation.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that a high-capacity link (e.g., 1 Gbps) automatically delivers high throughput, without realizing protocol behavior like stop-and-wait can cap effective throughput far below link rate (e.g., 267 kbps).
Computing utilization using only the transmission time L/R and neglecting the round-trip propagation delay that dominates the sender's idle time.
Assuming stop-and-wait is acceptable in general because it is simple, rather than recognizing it wastes most of the channel on high bandwidth-delay product paths.
Thinking the low-utilization problem is solved by buying faster links, when in fact the fix requires allowing multiple unacknowledged packets in flight (pipelining).

children.title: Go-Back-N (GBN) Protocol
children.summary: Pipelined sliding-window protocol allowing up to N unacknowledged packets, using cumulative ACKs and retransmitting all outstanding packets after a single timeout; the receiver discards out-of-order packets.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain the operation of the Go-Back-N protocol, including its window of at most N unacknowledged packets, its use of cumulative acknowledgments, and its retransmission of all outstanding packets after a timeout.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often think the GBN receiver buffers correctly received out-of-order packets, when in fact it discards them because data must be delivered in order to the upper layer.
A common error is believing GBN acknowledges each packet individually, when it actually uses cumulative acknowledgments indicating that all packets with sequence numbers up to k have been received.
Students may assume that after a packet loss GBN retransmits only the lost packet, when it actually retransmits all outstanding packets after a timeout.
Students sometimes think the GBN sender can transmit packets without waiting for acknowledgments indefinitely, when it is constrained to no more than N unacknowledged packets in the pipeline.

children.title: Selective Repeat (SR) Protocol
children.summary: Pipelined protocol in which the receiver individually acknowledges and buffers out-of-order packets while the sender retransmits only missing packets; covers per-packet timers and window-size constraints relative to the sequence-number space.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how the Selective Repeat protocol uses individual acknowledgments, receiver buffering of out-of-order packets, and per-packet timers to retransmit only lost or corrupted packets, and can determine why the window size is constrained relative to the sequence-number space.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that, like GBN, SR retransmits all outstanding packets after a single loss, when in fact SR retransmits only the packets suspected of being lost or corrupted.
Assuming SR acknowledgments are cumulative, when the receiver must individually acknowledge each correctly received packet.
Assuming the sender and receiver windows always coincide, when lost ACKs mean the two sides can hold different views of what was received correctly.

Believing the SR window can be as large as the entire sequence-number space, when a window size close to the sequence range can cause the receiver to misidentify old retransmitted packets as new ones.

children.title: Connection-Oriented Transport: TCP
children.summary: The TCP connection (three-way handshake and teardown), TCP segment structure, round-trip time estimation and timeout management, TCP's reliable data transfer mechanisms, and flow control with the receive window.

children.title: The TCP Connection
children.summary: Why TCP is connection-oriented: the two processes must handshake before sending data, and each end maintains connection state (buffers, variables, sequence numbers). Covers point-to-point, full-duplex service and the maximum segment size (MSS).
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe a TCP connection as a point-to-point, full-duplex pipe between two processes and explain why a handshake and per-connection state are required before data transfer.

common_misconceptions.description: The learner believes that, like UDP, a TCP sender can immediately transmit application data without first establishing a connection with the receiving process.
The learner thinks TCP can deliver data from one sender to many receivers in a single send operation, when in fact TCP is strictly point-to-point between two hosts.
The learner assumes full-duplex service requires two separate connections, one per direction, rather than a single connection whose socket at each end both sends and receives bytes.
The learner believes connection state such as buffers and sequence numbers is maintained only at the sending side, when in fact both endpoints of the connection maintain state.

children.title: TCP Segment Structure
children.summary: Anatomy of the TCP segment: source/destination port numbers, 32-bit sequence and acknowledgment numbers (byte-stream offsets), header flags (ACK, RST, SYN, FIN), receive window, checksum, options, and data payload.
children.learning_objective: The learner can identify the fields of a TCP segment (header fields plus data field) and explain how sequence and acknowledgment numbers operate as byte-stream offsets rather than segment counters.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing TCP sequence numbers identify segments themselves, when they actually give the byte-stream number of the first byte of data in the segment.
Assuming application data is packed into the header fields, when the TCP segment is composed of a separate header fields section and a data field.
Thinking the TCP header is as minimal as UDP's four two-byte fields, when the TCP header includes many fields such as ports, sequence/acknowledgment numbers, flags, receive window, and checksum.
Assuming TCP connection state like buffers and variables is allocated in intermediate network elements, when it exists only in the end hosts.

children.title: RTT Estimation and Timeout
children.summary: How TCP measures SampleRTT and computes EstimatedRTT and DevRTT using exponential weighted moving averages, sets TimeoutInterval, and doubles the timeout after a retransmission timeout.
children.learning_objective: The learner can compute TCP's EstimatedRTT, DevRTT, and TimeoutInterval from SampleRTT measurements using the exponential weighted moving average formulas and explain why SampleRTT is only measured for segments transmitted once.

common_misconceptions.description: TCP does not measure SampleRTT for every transmitted segment; it takes only one measurement at a time and never measures SampleRTT for retransmitted segments (Karn's algorithm).
The timeout interval should not be set exactly equal to EstimatedRTT; TCP adds a margin of 4 x DevRTT so the timeout is larger than EstimatedRTT yet still allows quick retransmission.
DevRTT is not an average of the SampleRTT values themselves; it is an EWMA of the absolute difference between SampleRTT and EstimatedRTT, reflecting fluctuation rather than the mean.
The EWMA formulas do not weight all SampleRTT values equally; recent samples influence EstimatedRTT more, with the recommended weighting factor alpha = 0.125 (and beta = 0.25 for DevRTT).

children.title: TCP Reliable Data Transfer
children.summary: How TCP provides reliability over an unreliable IP layer: cumulative acknowledgments, a single retransmission timer, sender events (ACK receipt, timeout, retransmission), and fast retransmit triggered by three duplicate ACKs.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how TCP provides reliable data transfer over IP's unreliable best-effort service, including cumulative acknowledgments, a single retransmission timer, sender events (ACK receipt, timeout, retransmission), and fast retransmit after three duplicate ACKs.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing TCP runs a separate retransmission timer for every outstanding segment, when in fact recommended TCP procedures use only a single retransmission timer even with multiple unacknowledged segments.
Thinking a single duplicate ACK triggers fast retransmit, when fast retransmit is triggered only after three duplicate ACKs are received.
Assuming IP guarantees delivery, ordering, or data integrity, when IP is unreliable and TCP must build reliability on top of it.
Believing TCP recovers lost segments only via timeouts, when TCP also uses duplicate acknowledgments as an additional recovery mechanism.

children.title: TCP Flow Control
children.summary: The speed-matching service that prevents the sender from overflowing the receiver's buffer: the receive window (rwnd) advertised in segment headers and how the sender limits unacknowledged data to this window.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how TCP's flow-control service uses the receiver-advertised window (rwnd) to limit the sender's unacknowledged data so the receiver's buffer is not overflowed.

common_misconceptions.description: Flow control and congestion control are interchangeable terms, when in fact both throttle the sender but for very different reasons (receiver buffer space vs. network congestion).
The receive window is the only constraint on the sender, when in fact the amount of unacknowledged data is limited by the minimum of cwnd and rwnd.
A sender may transmit as fast as it wants as long as segments are eventually acknowledged, ignoring that unacknowledged data must stay within the advertised receive window.
The receiving application reads data from the receive buffer as soon as it arrives, when in reality it may read slowly or not at all, which is exactly why the buffer can overflow.

children.title: TCP Connection Management
children.summary: The connection lifecycle: the three-way handshake (SYN, SYN+ACK, ACK) with sequence number selection, connection teardown using FIN segments and ACKs, and the resulting client/server state transitions.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe how a TCP connection is established and torn down, including the handshake and FIN/ACK message exchanges and the resulting client/server state transitions.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing the handshaking procedure is optional overhead, when in fact it is an integral part of TCP's connection-oriented service that must precede data flow.
Assuming TCP connection establishment has no performance cost, when it can significantly add to perceived delays, for example when surfing the Web.
Thinking TCP connection management involves only data transfer, overlooking that it can be exploited by attacks such as the SYN flood.
Assuming every connection socket corresponds one-to-one with a separate process, when high-performance Web servers often use one process with a new thread and socket per client connection.

children.title: Congestion Control
children.summary: The causes and costs of network congestion, network-assisted versus end-to-end control approaches, and TCP's approach to congestion control (slow start, congestion avoidance/AIMD, fast recovery) along with fairness considerations.

children.title: Causes and Costs of Congestion
children.summary: Walks through three increasingly complex scenarios (two senders sharing a router with infinite buffers, finite buffers, and multiple senders on a multihop path) to show why congestion occurs and what it costs: growing queuing delay, packet loss, retransmissions, wasted link capacity, and congestion collapse.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain, using the three increasingly complex scenarios, why network congestion occurs and identify its costs (queuing delay, packet loss, retransmissions, wasted router work, and throughput collapse).

common_misconceptions.description: Students often think increasing offered load always increases delivered throughput, but when the sending rate exceeds link capacity (R/2 per connection in scenario 1), throughput caps at R/2 regardless of load.
Students may believe a fully utilized link is the ideal state, overlooking that as the link approaches capacity, queuing delay grows unboundedly even without loss.
Students often assume lost packets simply disappear with no cost, not realizing retransmissions consume link capacity and can drop goodput to R/3 when half the traffic is retransmitted duplicates.
Students may think congestion only matters when buffers overflow, missing that premature timeouts cause duplicate deliveries that waste router forwarding work even without loss.

children.title: End-to-End vs. Network-Assisted Approaches
children.summary: Distinguishes the two broad approaches by whether the network layer provides explicit assistance: end-to-end control, where end systems must infer congestion from observed loss or delay (as TCP does), versus network-assisted control, where the network supplies explicit congestion feedback (e.g., explicit congestion notification).
children.learning_objective: The learner can distinguish between end-to-end congestion control, where end systems infer congestion from observed loss or delay, and network-assisted congestion control, where the network provides explicit congestion feedback such as explicit congestion notification.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that TCP relies on explicit congestion notifications from the network rather than inferring congestion from end-system observations like loss and delay.
Assuming a network can only use one approach, when in practice end-to-end and network-assisted mechanisms can coexist, e.g., TCP running over networks with explicit congestion notification.
