Thinking congestion control is handled solely by the network layer, when in the end-to-end approach the end systems themselves must detect and react to congestion.

children.title: Classic TCP Congestion Control
children.summary: How classic TCP (RFC 5681) implements end-to-end control since IP provides no explicit congestion feedback: the congestion window grows exponentially during slow start, then additively increases and multiplicatively decreases (AIMD) in congestion avoidance, with fast recovery on loss. Spans several mechanisms, so it should be split into slow start, congestion avoidance/AIMD, and fast recovery lessons.

children.title: Congestion Window and Loss Signals
children.summary: How classic TCP infers congestion end-to-end since IP gives no explicit feedback: the congestion window (cwnd) limits the sending rate, arriving ACKs signal a congestion-free path and permit increases, while loss events (triple duplicate ACKs vs. timeouts) signal congestion and trigger decreases.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how a classic TCP sender uses the congestion window, arriving ACKs, and loss events to infer path congestion and adjust its sending rate.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners may conflate the congestion window with the sending rate, when cwnd is an upper bound on unacknowledged data that only determines a rate in combination with the RTT.
Learners may believe an arriving ACK proves the entire end-to-end path is congestion-free, when it only indicates that the acknowledged segments were delivered without encountering congestion.
Learners may attribute packet loss to transmission errors rather than network congestion, whereas classic TCP treats every loss event as a signal of a congested path.
Learners may assume TCP reduces its rate the same way it increases it, when loss actually triggers a multiplicative decrease while congestion-free operation yields only additive increases.

children.title: Slow Start
children.summary: The initial slow-start phase: cwnd starts small and grows exponentially (doubling per RTT) as ACKs arrive, until the slow-start threshold (ssthresh) or a loss event ends the phase; also its contribution to connection latency.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe how TCP slow start exponentially grows the congestion window (doubling per RTT), identify when the phase ends (ssthresh or a loss event), and calculate the delay slow start contributes to object retrieval.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that the congestion window grows linearly during slow start, when in fact it doubles every RTT as each ACKed segment allows two more segments to be sent.
Thinking slow start continues for the lifetime of the connection, rather than ending when ssthresh is reached or a loss event occurs.
Assuming that a timeout-induced loss event only reduces cwnd (e.g., by half), when in fact the sender sets cwnd to 1 MSS and restarts slow start.
Overlooking that the small initial cwnd during slow start adds noticeable delay when transferring objects that require multiple segments.

children.title: Congestion Avoidance and AIMD
children.summary: The steady-state additive-increase, multiplicative-decrease (AIMD) behavior: cwnd grows linearly by 1 MSS per RTT and is halved on a triple duplicate-ACK loss, producing the saw-tooth pattern as TCP probes for the available bandwidth.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how TCP's AIMD algorithm additively increases cwnd by 1 MSS per RTT and multiplicatively halves it on a triple duplicate-ACK loss, and sketch the resulting saw-tooth pattern of probing for available bandwidth.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that TCP reduces cwnd by a fixed amount after loss, when AIMD actually halves (multiplicatively decreases) cwnd on a triple duplicate-ACK event.
Thinking cwnd grows by 1 MSS for every individual ACK received, rather than by 1 MSS per RTT (per round of ACKs) during additive increase.
Assuming all loss events trigger the same halving behavior, when the classic AIMD saw-tooth is defined for losses indicated by triple duplicate ACKs rather than timeouts.
Confusing the linear saw-tooth probing phase of AIMD with slow start's exponential growth of cwnd during connection startup.

children.title: Fast Recovery
children.summary: Reacting to loss without a timeout: fast retransmit of the missing segment after three duplicate ACKs, halving cwnd and continuing transmission (Reno-style fast recovery), contrasted with the timeout-driven reset to slow start (Tahoe).
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe TCP Reno's fast recovery—halving cwnd, setting ssthresh, and inflating cwnd by 1 MSS per duplicate ACK after a triple-duplicate-ACK loss event—and contrast it with Tahoe's timeout-driven cut to slow start.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing fast recovery is entered after a timeout, when it is actually entered after three duplicate ACKs indicate a less drastic loss event.
Assuming cwnd is cut to 1 MSS on a triple-duplicate-ACK loss, confusing Reno's halving behavior with Tahoe's unconditional reset to slow start.
Thinking fast recovery is a required part of TCP, when RFC 5681 only recommends it.
Assuming duplicate ACKs are ignored during fast recovery, when each duplicate ACK for the missing segment actually increases cwnd by 1 MSS.

children.title: AIMD Fairness
children.summary: Why AIMD yields an equal share of a congested link's bandwidth among competing TCP connections: the additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease dynamics converge competing flows toward equal throughput.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how the additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease dynamics of TCP congestion control converge competing connections toward an equal share of a congested link's bandwidth.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that multiplicative decrease makes competing flows more unequal, when in fact proportional halving moves flows with different window sizes toward equal values.
Assuming additive increase benefits larger flows more, when the equal absolute increase per RTT is precisely what pushes competing flows toward equal throughput.
Interpreting the saw-tooth oscillation of cwnd as evidence of unfairness, rather than as the probing-for-bandwidth behavior that accompanies AIMD's convergence to fairness.
Assuming AIMD guarantees equal throughput in all conditions, ignoring that factors like different round-trip times can prevent competing flows from achieving equal shares.

children.title: Fairness of TCP Congestion Control
children.summary: Examines how AIMD strives to give each TCP connection passing through a congested link an equal share of the link bandwidth, the sawtooth convergence toward equal shares, and behaviors such as synchronization of competing connections' window sizes.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how AIMD congestion control converges toward an equal share of bottleneck link bandwidth among competing TCP connections and identify factors that undermine this fairness.

common_misconceptions.description: TCP AIMD always achieves equal bandwidth shares in practice, when in reality unequal RTTs and differing conditions mean connections can obtain very unequal portions of link bandwidth.

Additive increase and multiplicative decrease cause connections to drift apart, when in fact the sawtooth pattern drives competing connections' window sizes toward convergence on the equal-share line.

Using multiple parallel TCP connections is fair behavior, when in fact an application using N parallel connections obtains a larger fraction of the bottleneck bandwidth than a single-connection application.
Fairness concerns only apply to TCP, when in fact UDP-based multimedia applications without congestion control can also consume unfair shares of bottleneck bandwidth.

children.title: Newer TCP Variants: Delay-Based and ECN
children.summary: Surveys newer flavors of TCP that determine the sending rate more quickly than classic loss-based TCP by using a delay-based approach or explicit congestion notification (ECN) from the network rather than inferring congestion purely from loss.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how newer TCP variants determine the sending rate more quickly than classic loss-based TCP by using delay-based congestion inference or explicit congestion notification (ECN) from the network.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners often think ECN-capable TCP still relies on packet loss to detect congestion, when in fact the network explicitly signals congestion to the sender and receiver.
Learners may believe delay-based TCP infers congestion the same way classic TCP does, rather than using measured packet delay as the congestion signal.
Learners may assume ECN is a TCP-only change, when it actually requires extensions to both IP and TCP (RFC 3168).
Learners may think newer TCP variants react to congestion at the same pace as classic loss-based TCP, when their purpose is to determine the sending rate more quickly.

children.title: Impact of Slow Start on Latency
children.summary: Analyzes how TCP connection establishment and slow start significantly contribute to end-to-end delay in many important scenarios, which motivates designs that determine the sending rate more quickly.
children.learning_objective: The learner can quantify how TCP connection establishment and the slow-start phase contribute to end-to-end delay when retrieving an object, given segment size, link rate, and RTT.

common_misconceptions.description: Despite its name, slow start actually increases the congestion window (and thus the sending rate) exponentially and rapidly, so learners may wrongly assume it always imposes a large delay penalty.
Learners often assume TCP begins sending at full link rate, not realizing the initial sending rate is roughly MSS/RTT because cwnd starts at 1 MSS.
Learners may think object retrieval time is just a few RTTs and ignore that connection establishment and the slowly ramping window add significant delay, especially for short transfers.

children.title: Forwarding vs. Routing in the Network Layer
children.summary: Introduces the two key network-layer functions: forwarding, the per-router data-plane function that moves a datagram from an input link to an output link, and routing, the control-plane, network-wide function that determines the end-to-end path a datagram takes from source to destination host.
children.learning_objective: The learner can distinguish forwarding as the per-router, data-plane function that moves a datagram from an input link to an output link from routing as the network-wide, control-plane function that determines the end-to-end path from sender to receiver.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often treat forwarding and routing as interchangeable names for the same function, when in fact forwarding is a local data-plane action and routing is a network-wide control-plane function.

Students may believe a single router computes the entire end-to-end path, when path determination is done by routing algorithms in the control plane and each router only forwards packets to the appropriate output link.
Students may confuse destination-based forwarding with path selection, thinking the forwarding function decides the route a packet takes rather than just the next output link.
Students may think the control plane directly moves datagrams, when it only computes and distributes the forwarding tables that the data plane uses to actually move packets.

children.title: Router Input and Output Ports
children.summary: Covers the internal operations of a router's input and output ports: how arriving packets are processed and looked up on input links, and how packets are prepared and transmitted onto output links.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the functions performed by a router's input ports (link termination, link-layer processing, and forwarding-table lookup) and explain how packets are forwarded from input ports to output ports via the switching fabric.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often believe the forwarding-table lookup is performed by the central routing processor, when in fact it is performed at the input port itself.
Students may think input and output ports only terminate the physical link, overlooking that they also perform link-layer functions and the lookup function.

Students may assume packets are always switched from input to output ports under direct control of the CPU, not knowing modern routers use memory, bus, or crossbar switching fabrics with processing on line cards.
Students may think the 'match plus action' paradigm of looking up a destination and forwarding is unique to routers, when it also appears in link-layer switches and firewalls.

children.title: Switching Fabric and Packet Queues
children.summary: Examines a router's internal switching mechanisms that move packets from input ports to output ports, and packet queue management, including where queues form inside a router and how they are managed.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how a router's switching fabric moves packets from input ports to output ports and analyze where and why packet queues form at input and output ports, including queue management policies such as drop-tail and active queue management.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often believe a faster switching fabric eliminates all queuing, when in fact even with R_switch N times faster than R_line, queuing can still occur at output ports when multiple inputs send to the same output.
Students may think packet queues form only at output ports, overlooking that input queuing can also occur when the switching fabric transfer rate is insufficient.

Students often assume packets are only dropped once the buffer is completely full, not realizing proactive policies like AQM can drop or mark packets (e.g., via ECN) before the buffer fills to signal congestion.
Students may treat memory, bus, and crossbar switching fabrics as equivalent, ignoring their different scaling capabilities and queuing delay behaviors.

children.title: Traditional IP Forwarding
children.summary: Covers destination-based forwarding, where a router forwards a datagram based on the destination address in the datagram's header by matching it against entries in the forwarding table.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how traditional IP forwarding works, where a router forwards a datagram by matching the destination address in its header against entries in the forwarding table.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing the router must examine and match the entire destination IP address, when in fact it matches only a portion (prefix) of the destination address.
Confusing the per-router data-plane forwarding function with the network-wide control-plane routing function that computes paths.
Assuming traditional IP forwarding uses multiple header fields, when it is actually based solely on the datagram's destination address, unlike generalized forwarding.
Thinking forwarding tables only contain exact destination addresses rather than address prefixes that can match ranges of destination addresses.

children.title: Generalized Forwarding
children.summary: Covers generalized forwarding, in which forwarding and other packet-processing functions are performed using values from several different fields in the datagram's header rather than the destination address alone.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain the match-plus-action paradigm of generalized forwarding, in which packets are processed based on multiple header fields at different layers and can be forwarded, dropped, or have fields modified.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that forwarding decisions can only be based on the destination IP address, when generalized forwarding matches on multiple header fields from different protocol layers.
Assuming forwarding is the only possible action, when matched packets may also be dropped, encapsulated and sent to a remote controller, broadcast/multicast, or have header fields rewritten.
Thinking that match decisions are confined to a single layer, when matching can span layer 2, 3, and 4 header fields in the protocol stack.
Assuming flow tables are computed locally by each device, when in SDN they are computed, installed, and updated by a remote controller.

children.title: Software-Defined Networking (SDN)
children.summary: Describes how SDN explicitly separates the data plane from the control plane: the routing device performs forwarding only, while a remote, software-implemented controller computes and distributes forwarding tables to the routers.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the SDN architecture in which the data plane (forwarding in switches/routers) is separated from the control plane (a remote, software-implemented controller that computes and distributes forwarding tables), and identify its key characteristics.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often think SDN is synonymous with OpenFlow, when OpenFlow is just one standard protocol used to tell switches what to do.
Students may assume the controller resides inside each router, not realizing SDN explicitly places control in a remote, logically centralized software controller (e.g., in a data center).
Students may believe SDN forwarding decisions use only network-layer addresses, when SDN switches can match on transport-, network-, and link-layer header fields.
Students may think SDN control software must come from the equipment vendor, whereas it can be written by many different programmers independently of switch hardware.

children.title: Control Plane Approaches: Per-Router vs. SDN
children.summary: Introduces the network-wide logic that controls how datagrams are routed end-to-end and how network-layer services are configured and managed. Contrasts the two broad approaches: traditional per-router control, where a routing algorithm runs in every router and routers communicate routing information with each other, and software-defined networking (SDN) control, where a logically centralized controller computes and distributes forwarding tables to all routers.
children.learning_objective: The learner can contrast the traditional per-router control plane approach, where each router runs a routing algorithm and exchanges routing information with other routers, with the SDN approach, where a logically centralized controller computes and distributes forwarding tables to all routers.

common_misconceptions.description: SDN eliminates routers entirely, when in fact routers still perform forwarding and only the computation and distribution of forwarding tables moves to a remote controller.
In per-router control, each router operates independently without communicating, when actually the routing components in routers exchange routing information with each other.
The SDN controller must be a single physical device, when it is only logically centralized and can be implemented in a remote data center with high reliability and redundancy.
Least-cost routing algorithms like link-state and distance-vector apply only to per-router control, when they find application in both per-router and SDN control.

children.title: Link-State (LS) Routing Algorithm
children.summary: Covers the link-state routing algorithm for computing least-cost paths in a graph, in which each node has complete knowledge of network topology and link costs and runs a centralized algorithm (e.g., Dijkstra's) to compute least-cost paths from itself to all other nodes.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain the link-state routing algorithm, including how each node uses complete topology knowledge to run Dijkstra's algorithm and compute least-cost paths to all other nodes.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that LS algorithms are decentralized, when in fact each node has complete information about connectivity and link costs and runs a centralized algorithm.
Thinking Dijkstra's algorithm computes all least-cost paths in a single step, rather than iteratively, with least-cost paths to k destinations known after the kth iteration.
Assuming a node only needs knowledge of its directly attached links to run an LS algorithm, confusing it with decentralized (distance-vector) algorithms.
Believing all routers should run the LS algorithm at the same time, whereas synchronization can be problematic and routers can even self-synchronize unintentionally.

children.title: Distance-Vector (DV) Routing Algorithm
children.summary: Covers the distance-vector routing algorithm, a distributed, asynchronous, iterative approach based on the Bellman-Ford equation, in which each node maintains a vector of least-cost estimates to all destinations and exchanges these vectors with its directly connected neighbors.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how the distance-vector routing algorithm works as an iterative, asynchronous, distributed algorithm based on the Bellman-Ford equation, including how nodes exchange vectors with neighbors and derive forwarding-table next hops.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often think the DV algorithm requires global knowledge of all link costs, when in fact each node only knows costs of its directly attached links and learns from neighbors iteratively.
Students may believe the shortest-path distance itself is what goes in the forwarding table, when actually the node needs the next-hop router v*(y) that achieves the minimum.
Students may think all nodes must operate in lockstep (synchronously), when the DV algorithm is asynchronous and self-terminating without any explicit stop signal.
Students may assume every node sends its distance vector after each recomputation, when a node only sends updates if its distance vector has changed.

children.title: Intra-AS Routing: OSPF
children.summary: Covers OSPF, the widely deployed intra-AS routing protocol that operates within a single ISP's network (autonomous system), including how it implements link-state routing inside an administrative domain.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how OSPF implements link-state routing within a single autonomous system, including flooding of link-state information, Dijkstra's shortest-path computation, administrator-configured link costs, and hierarchical routing using areas and area border routers.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often think OSPF link-state information is sent only to directly attached neighbors, when in fact it is flooded so every router in the area builds a complete topological map of the AS.
Students may assume OSPF link costs are computed automatically by the protocol, when they are actually configured by the network administrator.
Students may believe every autonomous system must use the same intra-AS routing algorithm, though each AS can choose its own (e.g., OSPF or EIGRP).
Students may think OSPF runs as one flat link-state domain, missing that an AS can be hierarchically configured into areas with area border routers and a backbone area for inter-area traffic.

children.title: Inter-AS Routing: BGP
children.summary: Covers BGP, the routing protocol that serves to interconnect all of the networks in the Internet, providing routing between autonomous systems and scaling routing across the entire Internet.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how BGP enables inter-AS routing by advertising CIDRized prefix reachability between autonomous systems and describe key attributes like AS-PATH and NEXT-HOP.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often think BGP routes packets to individual destination addresses, when in fact BGP routes to CIDRized prefixes representing subnets or collections of subnets.
Students may believe BGP determines routes within an AS, when intra-AS routing protocols like OSPF handle internal routing and BGP only handles routing across multiple ASs.
Students may think BGP chooses loop-free paths by design, when actually loop prevention relies on a router rejecting any advertisement whose AS-PATH already contains its own AS number.
Students often overlook that the NEXT-HOP attribute, the IP address of the router interface beginning the AS-PATH, provides the critical link between inter-AS and intra-AS routing.

children.title: SDN Control Plane: Controller and Applications
children.summary: Covers the architecture of the SDN control plane, divided into the SDN controller and SDN network-control applications. Emphasizes the separation of data plane (simple, fast switches executing match-plus-action rules in flow tables) and control plane (servers and software that compute, manage, and install flow table entries in all switches).
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the two components of the SDN control plane — the SDN controller and the SDN network-control applications — and explain how the controller computes, manages, and installs flow table entries in switches, distinguishing this from traditional per-router control.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often believe the logically centralized controller is a single physical server, when in practice it is implemented by a distributed set of servers for fault tolerance, availability, and performance.

Students may think SDN switches compute their own forwarding decisions, when in fact they are simple, fast devices that merely execute the match-plus-action rules installed in their flow tables by the control plane.

Students may conflate SDN control with traditional per-router control, not realizing that in SDN a logically centralized controller computes and distributes forwarding tables to all routers rather than routing algorithms running in each router.
Students may view the controller and its network-control applications as one monolithic service, when the control plane is divided into distinct controller and application components.

children.title: Network Management: NETCONF and YANG
children.summary: Covers configuration and management of network-layer devices using the NETCONF protocol, which exchanges XML-encoded RPC messages (e.g., edit-config commands and replies) between a managing server and managed devices, and the YANG data modeling language used to specify the structure and syntax of configuration data.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe how the NETCONF protocol exchanges XML-encoded RPC messages (such as <edit-config> commands and OK replies) between a managing server and managed devices, and explain YANG's role as a data modeling language for configuration data.

common_misconceptions.description: Confusing YANG with a communication protocol, when it is actually a data modeling language used to specify the structure and syntax of configuration and operational data, while NETCONF is the protocol that communicates it.
Assuming NETCONF messages are plain-text commands, rather than XML-encoded RPC messages carrying commands like <edit-config> and structured replies such as <ok/>.

Believing NETCONF/YANG is just another name for SNMP, when it instead takes a more abstract, network-wide, holistic approach with stronger emphasis on configuration management, correctness constraints, and atomic multi-device operations.
Thinking a successful NETCONF configuration change returns the new configuration data, when the managed device simply responds with an OK reply inside an XML rpc-reply document.

children.title: Introduction to the Link Layer
children.summary: The basic service of moving network-layer datagrams between adjacent nodes via framing/encapsulation; the services provided (link access, reliable delivery, error detection) and where the link layer is implemented (network adapters/NICs); broadcast vs. point-to-point links.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain the link layer's basic service of moving network-layer datagrams between adjacent nodes via frame encapsulation, identify the services it provides, and distinguish broadcast from point-to-point links.

common_misconceptions.description: The link layer moves datagrams across the entire end-to-end path, when in fact its basic service is only to move datagrams between adjacent nodes.
Network-layer datagrams are transmitted directly over a link, when in fact all link-layer protocols encapsulate the datagram within a link-layer frame before transmission.
All link-layer protocols provide the same link-access, delivery, and error-detection services, when in fact different protocols offer very different services.
Coordinating access to broadcast links and point-to-point links is equally complex, when in fact coordinating access to a point-to-point link is simpler.

children.title: Error-Detection and -Correction Techniques
children.summary: Techniques for detecting and correcting transmission errors in link-layer frames: simple and two-dimensional parity checks, checksumming methods, and the cyclic redundancy check (CRC).
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how error-detection and -correction (EDC) bits protect link-layer frames and compare parity checks, two-dimensional parity, checksumming, and CRC in terms of detection/correction capability and overhead.

common_misconceptions.description: Detecting that bit errors occurred does not mean the receiver can correct them; correction requires extra redundancy, such as two-dimensional parity or forward error correction (FEC).
Error-detection bits cannot guarantee that every corrupted frame is caught, so an undetected error may still cause a corrupted datagram to be delivered to the network layer.
More sophisticated error-detection schemes are not free: they incur larger overhead because more EDC bits must be computed and transmitted.
One-bit parity can only detect certain bit errors, whereas the two-dimensional parity scheme adds row and column parity that lets the receiver locate and correct a single-bit error.

children.title: Multiple Access Protocols
children.summary: Coordinating access to a shared broadcast channel using three broad approaches: channel partitioning (TDM, FDM), random access (ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD), and taking-turns (polling, token passing); DOCSIS as the link-layer protocol for cable Internet access.

children.title: The Multiple Access Problem
children.summary: Why shared broadcast channels need coordination: when multiple nodes transmit at the same time, frames collide, all colliding frames are lost, and the channel is wasted during the collision interval.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain why simultaneous transmissions on a shared broadcast channel collide, why all colliding frames are lost, and why this necessitates coordination via multiple access protocols.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that only one of the colliding frames is lost, when in fact all frames involved in a collision are lost.
Assuming receivers can still make sense of frames during a collision, when the colliding signals become inextricably tangled and unintelligible.
Thinking the broadcast channel remains productive during a collision, when it is actually wasted for the entire collision interval.
Assuming nodes can transmit on a shared broadcast channel whenever they like without any coordination mechanism, ignoring the need for multiple access protocols.

children.title: Channel Partitioning: TDM and FDM
children.summary: Dividing the broadcast channel among nodes by time slots (TDM) or frequency bands (FDM) so each node gets a dedicated portion of the channel and collisions are avoided.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how TDM and FDM partition a broadcast channel of rate R bps among N nodes and evaluate their advantages (collision avoidance, fair division) and drawbacks (each node limited to R/N even when alone with packets to send).

common_misconceptions.description: Confusing the TDM time frame (a repeating structure of N time slots) with the link-layer frame, which is the unit of data exchanged between adapters.
Believing a node can use the full channel rate R when other nodes are idle, when in fact TDM and FDM limit every node to R/N regardless of demand.
Assuming channel partitioning uses bandwidth efficiently, when in reality slots or frequency bands go unused (are wasted) whenever their assigned node has nothing to send.
Thinking collisions can still happen under TDM or FDM, even though each node transmits in its own dedicated time slot or frequency band, so collisions are avoided.

children.title: Slotted ALOHA
children.summary: The simplest random access protocol: time is divided into synchronized slots of one frame-transmission time, nodes transmit with probability p at slot beginnings, and colliding frames in a slot are all lost.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the operation of slotted ALOHA (synchronized slots, transmission with probability p at slot beginnings, all colliding frames lost) and explain why its maximum efficiency is only 1/e ≈ 37% of slots.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing the channel achieves its full R bps transmission rate, when in fact at best only 37% of slots do useful work, yielding an effective rate of about 0.37R.
Thinking that a slot with multiple transmissions can still deliver one of the frames, when in reality all frames that collide in a slot are lost.
Confusing efficiency with per-node throughput or single-node performance, when efficiency is defined as the long-run fraction of successful slots with many always-backlogged active nodes.
Assuming slotted ALOHA works without clock synchronization, when it specifically requires all nodes to know when slots begin (unlike pure ALOHA and CSMA).

children.title: CSMA and CSMA/CD
children.summary: Improving random access with carrier sensing (transmit only when the channel is idle) and collision detection with backoff; the efficiency of CSMA/CD depends on the ratio of maximum propagation time to frame transmission time.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how carrier sensing and collision detection with random backoff work in CSMA/CD, why collisions still occur despite sensing, and how CSMA/CD efficiency depends on the ratio of maximum propagation delay to frame transmission time.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that carrier sensing alone eliminates collisions, when in fact propagation delay can make a node sense an idle channel while another node's transmission is already underway.
Assuming a node detects a collision the instant it starts transmitting, when detection actually takes time related to the propagation delay between the colliding nodes.
Thinking the post-collision backoff wait is a fixed duration, when the adapter actually waits a random K times 512 bit times with K drawn randomly.
Assuming CSMA/CD efficiency is independent of channel geometry, when it in fact depends on the ratio of maximum propagation time (dprop) to frame transmission time (dtrans).

children.title: Taking-Turns: Polling and Token Passing
children.summary: Coordinating channel access by having a master node poll each node in round-robin fashion (polling) or by exchanging a control token that grants transmission rights (token passing).
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how the polling and token-passing protocols coordinate channel access in a round-robin fashion and identify their key drawbacks, including polling delay and master-node failure.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that token passing, like polling, requires a designated master node to coordinate transmissions, when in fact token passing operates without any master node.
Assuming a single active node transmits at the full rate R bps under polling, when in reality the master must poll each inactive node in turn, reducing the active node's effective rate.
Thinking that polling continues to work if the master node fails, when in fact the entire channel becomes inoperative upon master failure.
Mistaking the token for a data-carrying frame, when it is a small, special-purpose frame that merely grants a node the right to transmit.

children.title: DOCSIS Cable Access
children.summary: Case study of cable Internet access: the CMTS coordinates thousands of cable modems using FDM for downstream and upstream channels plus regulated upstream transmission, combining aspects of all three multiple access classes.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how DOCSIS cable access networks coordinate thousands of cable modems with a CMTS by combining FDM channel partitioning, TDM-like mini-slots, and CMTS-granted upstream transmission.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing the downstream channel faces a multiple access collision problem because many modems receive it, when in fact only the single CMTS transmits downstream so no collisions can occur.

Thinking DOCSIS coordinates access using only FDM, when the upstream direction is additionally divided into TDM-like intervals of mini-slots in which the CMTS explicitly grants modems permission to transmit.
Assuming upstream transmissions are always collision-free because the CMTS schedules them, when multiple modems sharing the same upstream channel can still potentially collide.
Believing the CMTS is a unique device with no analogue elsewhere, when it serves a function similar to the DSLAM in DSL networks by converting analog signals from many modems for Internet transport.

children.title: Link-Layer Addressing and ARP
children.summary: Link-layer (MAC) addresses, how they differ from network-layer addresses, and why broadcast channels require node addressing; address resolution between IP and MAC addresses.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how link-layer (MAC) addresses differ from network-layer (IP) addresses and describe how ARP resolves IP addresses to MAC addresses using broadcast queries and cached ARP tables with TTL-based expiration.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often think MAC and IP addresses are interchangeable or that only one kind of address is needed, when in fact link-layer addresses differ in size, structure, and scope from network-layer addresses and both are required.

Students frequently assume ARP belongs entirely to either the link layer or the network layer, when it actually sits between them: an ARP packet is encapsulated in a link-layer frame yet carries network-layer address fields.
Students may believe ARP tables must be configured by a system administrator, when ARP is plug-and-play: tables are built automatically and entries expire (typically after about 20 minutes).
Students often assume both the ARP query and the ARP response are sent in broadcast frames, when only the query is broadcast while the response is sent in a standard (unicast) frame.

children.title: Ethernet and Link-Layer Switches
children.summary: Ethernet framing and link-layer technologies; how link-layer switches forward and filter frames (e.g., self-learning) and their role compared with routers.

children.title: Link-Layer Addressing and ARP
children.summary: Link-layer (MAC) addresses and how they differ from network-layer IP addresses; the ARP protocol for resolving IP-to-MAC addresses; sending datagrams to nodes off the local subnet.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how link-layer (MAC) addresses differ from network-layer (IP) addresses and describe how ARP resolves IP addresses to MAC addresses using broadcast queries and cached ARP tables with TTL-based expiration.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often think MAC and IP addresses are interchangeable or that only one kind of address is needed, when in fact link-layer addresses differ in size, structure, and scope from network-layer addresses and both are required.

Students frequently assume ARP belongs entirely to either the link layer or the network layer, when it actually sits between them: an ARP packet is encapsulated in a link-layer frame yet carries network-layer address fields.
Students may believe ARP tables must be configured by a system administrator, when ARP is plug-and-play: tables are built automatically and entries expire (typically after about 20 minutes).
Students often assume both the ARP query and the ARP response are sent in broadcast frames, when only the query is broadcast while the response is sent in a standard (unicast) frame.

children.title: Ethernet: Frame Format and Evolution
children.summary: The structure of the Ethernet frame (data field, source/destination addresses, type field, CRC) and Ethernet's history and enduring dominance as the standard LAN technology.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how the Ethernet frame format and MAC protocol have been preserved across successive speed standards and decode the naming conventions (speed, BASE, media) of IEEE 802.3 Ethernet standards.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that each new Ethernet speed (e.g., 100 Mbps) required a completely new frame format, when in fact the original MAC protocol and frame format were preserved while only the physical layers changed.
Treating Ethernet standard names like 100BASE-TX or 10GBASE-T as meaningless labels, when each part encodes the speed, baseband transmission, and physical medium.
Assuming that switched, full-duplex Ethernet at gigabit speeds is so different from the original Metcalfe-Boggs design that it is no longer Ethernet, when it remains Ethernet by definition.
Thinking that running Ethernet over a different physical medium (copper vs. fiber) changes the frame format, when different physical layers share a common link-layer MAC protocol and frame format.

children.title: Switch Forwarding, Filtering, and Self-Learning
children.summary: How a switch uses its switch table to forward or filter incoming frames based on destination MAC addresses, and how it builds and ages table entries automatically via self-learning, making it a transparent plug-and-play device.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how a switch forwards or filters incoming frames based on destination MAC addresses and describe how the switch automatically builds its table through self-learning.

common_misconceptions.description: Students often believe the switch table must be populated by a network administrator or a configuration protocol, when in fact switches are self-learning and build their tables automatically, dynamically, and autonomously.
A common error is assuming switches forward frames using IP addresses like routers, when switches forward packets based on layer-2 destination MAC addresses.
Learners may think the switch table comes pre-loaded with host locations, when it actually starts empty and records the source MAC address, incoming interface, and time for each arriving frame.
Students may assume a traditional switch table is constructed the same way as a router's forwarding table, when the two are built in very different manners.

children.title: Properties of Link-Layer Switching
children.summary: Advantages of switches over broadcast links and hubs: eliminating collisions through dedicated per-host bandwidth, full-duplex send/receive on each interface, and simplified network administration.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how link-layer switching eliminates collisions by giving each host dedicated bandwidth and full-duplex interfaces, and why this simplifies network administration compared with shared broadcast links and hubs.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that switches forward all frames to every host like hubs, so collisions still occur on a switched LAN.
Assuming a switch interface can only transmit or receive at one time, when in fact each interface supports simultaneous full-duplex send and receive.

Thinking that adding more hosts to a shared broadcast channel does not reduce effective per-host throughput, ignoring that switched dedicated bandwidth avoids the efficiency loss of shared multiple-access channels.
Believing that a switched LAN is more complex to administer than a hub-based broadcast LAN, when switching actually simplifies network administration.

children.title: Switches versus Routers
children.summary: Comparing link-layer switches (implementing layers 1-2, forwarding on MAC addresses) with routers (implementing layers 1-3, forwarding on IP addresses), and the trade-offs in choosing between them.
children.learning_objective: The learner can compare link-layer switches and routers in terms of the layers they implement, the addresses they use to forward packets, and the trade-offs that determine when each should be used in a network.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that switches and routers are interchangeable because both are store-and-forward packet switches, when in fact switches forward on MAC addresses at layer 2 while routers forward on IP addresses at layer 3.
Assuming switches and routers process packets through the same layers, when switches only process frames up through layer 2 while routers must process datagrams up through layer 3.
Thinking a switched network can have an arbitrary topology with loops, when the active topology must be restricted to a spanning tree to prevent cycling of broadcast frames.

Believing switches alone suffice for networks of any size, when large networks with thousands of hosts typically need routers for traffic isolation, broadcast-storm control, and more intelligent routing.

children.title: Virtual LANs (VLANs)
children.summary: How multiple virtual LANs can be created over a single physical LAN/switch infrastructure, providing traffic isolation and flexible VLAN membership.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how VLANs enable traffic isolation and flexible membership on a single physical LAN infrastructure, and describe port-based, MAC-based, and protocol-based VLAN assignment methods.

common_misconceptions.description: VLANs require separate physical switches for each virtual LAN.
VLAN membership can only be assigned based on switch ports.
VLANs cannot be extended across IP routers to connect geographically separated LANs.

children.title: Virtual LANs (VLANs)
children.summary: Creating multiple virtual LANs over a single physical LAN infrastructure, including VLAN configuration and traffic isolation.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how VLANs enable traffic isolation and flexible membership on a single physical LAN infrastructure, and describe port-based, MAC-based, and protocol-based VLAN assignment methods.

common_misconceptions.description: VLANs require separate physical switches for each virtual LAN.
VLAN membership can only be assigned based on switch ports.
VLANs cannot be extended across IP routers to connect geographically separated LANs.

children.title: MPLS and Data Center Networking
children.summary: How MPLS networks provide link-layer services when interconnecting IP routers, and an overview of network designs for today's massive data centers.

children.title: MPLS Label Switching Fundamentals
children.summary: How MPLS works: fixed-length labels, label-switched routers, and forwarding based on labels and FECs rather than longest-prefix IP destination matching, allowing MPLS networks to provide link-layer services interconnecting IP routers.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how MPLS label-switched routers use fixed-length labels to forward packets without examining IP headers, and identify the key fields in an MPLS header.

common_misconceptions.description: MPLS replaces IP routing entirely, rather than working alongside it as a link-layer technology that interconnects IP routers.
MPLS labels are equivalent to IP addresses and carry the same semantic meaning for destination-based forwarding.
MPLS forwarding uses longest-prefix matching on IP addresses like traditional IP routing, instead of exact-match label lookups.

children.title: MPLS Traffic Engineering and Fast Restoration
children.summary: Using MPLS to override standard IP routing: steering traffic toward a destination along multiple explicit paths for policy or performance, plus fast reroute over precomputed failover paths in response to link failure.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how MPLS traffic engineering overrides standard IP routing to steer traffic along multiple explicit paths for policy or performance, and how fast restoration uses precomputed failover paths to quickly reroute traffic after a link failure.

common_misconceptions.description: Thinking MPLS traffic engineering is only used for policy reasons, while it also optimizes performance.
Believing fast restoration is the same as standard IP routing convergence, rather than using precomputed failover paths.
Assuming MPLS traffic engineering replaces underlying routing protocols instead of overriding their forwarding decisions.

children.title: Data Center Purposes and Traffic Types
children.summary: Why massive data centers exist (serving content, massively-parallel computing, cloud applications) and the two traffic types they must support: external client-to-host flows and internal host-to-host flows.
children.learning_objective: The learner can list the three primary purposes of data centers and describe the two types of traffic flows in a data center network.

common_misconceptions.description: Data centers only serve web content, ignoring massively-parallel computing and cloud applications.
Data center networks only handle external client-to-host traffic, overlooking internal host-to-host flows.
Border routers are not required for external client-to-host traffic.
Internal host-to-host traffic is negligible compared to external traffic.

children.title: Data Center Network Architecture
children.summary: Hierarchical data center network design: border routers, access routers, tier-1/2/3 switches, TOR switches and racks; redundancy of equipment and links for high availability; and partitioning subnets into VLANs to localize ARP broadcast traffic.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the hierarchical architecture of a data center network including border routers, access routers, tier switches, TOR switches, redundancy mechanisms, VLAN partitioning for ARP localization, and multi-path routing using ECMP.

common_misconceptions.description: Data center networks rely on single-path routing rather than multi-path routing for traffic distribution.
Data center network designs do not include redundant equipment and links for high availability.
VLANs in data centers are not used to partition subnets and localize ARP broadcast traffic.
Data center networks use a flat topology instead of a hierarchical design with multiple tiers of switches.

children.title: Multipath Routing in Data Centers
children.summary: Exploiting rich inter-tier connectivity with multipath routing: ECMP's randomized next-hop selection, finer-grained flow-level load balancing, and designs that split individual packets of a flow across multiple paths.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe how multipath routing exploits rich inter-tier connectivity in data centers, including ECMP's randomized next-hop selection and finer-grained flow-level or packet-level load balancing schemes.

common_misconceptions.description: ECMP uses a deterministic next-hop selection rather than randomized selection across equal-cost paths.
Multipath routing in data centers only operates at the flow level and cannot split individual packets of a flow across multiple paths.
Data center networks use single-path routing by default because of their hierarchical topology.

children.title: Trends in Data Center Networking
children.summary: Recent developments: modular data centers built from shipping containers with electrical/optical interconnects, cloud providers customizing their own adapters, switches, and protocols, and Amazon-style availability zones replicating data centers across nearby buildings for fault tolerance.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the key trends in data center networking including modular container-based designs with electrical/optical interconnects, cloud provider customization of network hardware and protocols, availability zones for fault tolerance, and multi-path routing techniques.

common_misconceptions.description: Modular data centers are merely shipping containers without specialized electrical/optical interconnect architectures.
Cloud providers rely solely on commercial off-the-shelf network equipment rather than customizing their own adapters, switches, and protocols.
Availability zones are geographically distant regions rather than nearby buildings within a few kilometers for synchronous replication.
Multi-path routing in data centers is only used for load balancing and not as a fundamental design principle for fault tolerance and bandwidth utilization.

children.title: Wireless Links and Network Characteristics
children.summary: How wireless links differ from wired links: signal attenuation and path loss, interference from other sources, multipath propagation, SNR and bit error rates, plus an introduction to CDMA as a shared-medium access protocol used in wireless networks.

children.title: Signal Attenuation and Path Loss
children.summary: Why wireless signal strength decreases: electromagnetic radiation attenuates as it passes through matter (e.g., walls) and disperses even in free space, so received power falls as sender-receiver distance grows.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how electromagnetic radiation attenuates when passing through matter and disperses in free space, causing path loss that reduces received signal strength as sender-receiver distance increases.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners may think attenuation only occurs when signals pass through obstacles, ignoring free-space path loss due to signal dispersion.
Learners may assume signal strength decreases linearly with distance rather than following an inverse-square or higher-order path loss model.
Learners may confuse signal attenuation (power loss over distance) with interference from other radio sources.
Learners may believe attenuation does not degrade the signal-to-noise ratio, overlooking that reduced signal power lowers SNR.

children.title: Interference and Multipath Propagation
children.summary: How wireless signals are corrupted by other radio sources transmitting in the same frequency band, and how reflections off objects cause multipath propagation where multiple copies of a signal arrive at the receiver.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how interference from other radio sources and multipath propagation due to reflections corrupt wireless signals, and describe the hidden terminal problem and fading effects.

common_misconceptions.description: Interference only originates from devices within the same wireless network.
Multipath propagation always degrades signal quality and never provides diversity gain.
The hidden terminal problem is equivalent to a standard collision in wired networks.
Signal fading is solely caused by increasing distance between transmitter and receiver.

children.title: SNR and Bit Error Rates
children.summary: The relationship between signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and bit error rate (BER) on a wireless link, and how changing channel conditions and distance cause bit errors.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe how signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) influences bit error rate (BER) and how different modulation techniques and distance affect this relationship.

common_misconceptions.description: SNR is an absolute measure of signal strength rather than a relative ratio of signal to noise.
Higher SNR always results in lower BER regardless of modulation technique.
BER is independent of the modulation technique used for a given SNR.

children.title: Wireless Link Rates and Coverage Ranges
children.summary: Comparison of the key characteristics of popular wireless network standards: their transmission rates and coverage distances, and how these vary with distance, channel conditions, and number of users.
children.learning_objective: The learner can compare the transmission rates and coverage ranges of popular wireless network standards and explain how these characteristics vary with distance, channel conditions, and the number of users.

common_misconceptions.description: Wireless link rates and coverage ranges are fixed values that do not change with environmental factors.
All wireless standards have similar transmission rates and coverage distances.
Transmission rates depend only on the wireless standard, not on distance, channel conditions, or number of users.
Coverage range represents the maximum distance at which any communication is possible, regardless of data rate.

children.title: CDMA: Code Division Multiple Access
children.summary: Introduction to CDMA as a shared-medium access protocol used in wireless networks, where senders encode their bits using unique code sequences so multiple users can transmit simultaneously over the same spectrum.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how CDMA enables multiple senders to transmit simultaneously over the same spectrum by assigning unique codes and how receivers recover original data bits using the additive property of interfering signals.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners may think any code sequence works, but CDMA codes must be carefully chosen to allow signal separation.
Learners may assume CDMA eliminates interference, but it manages interference through additive signal processing where multiple signals sum at the receiver.
Learners may confuse CDMA with TDM or FDM, but CDMA partitions the codespace, not time or frequency.

children.title: WiFi: 802.11 Wireless LANs
children.summary: The IEEE 802.11 (WiFi) standard: 802.11 architecture (BSS, access points, channels, SSIDs), the 802.11 MAC protocol (CSMA/CA), the 802.11 frame format, mobility within the same IP subnet, advanced features, and Bluetooth personal area networks.

children.title: 802.11 Architecture: BSS, APs, and Channels
children.summary: Covers the 802.11 standards family (b/g/n/ac/ax, branded WiFi 4/5/6), the basic service set (BSS), access points, channels and SSIDs, and how a station associates with an AP in a 'WiFi jungle' with multiple overlapping APs.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the 802.11 wireless LAN architecture including basic service sets (BSS), access points (APs), channels, and SSIDs, and explain how a station associates with an AP in an environment with multiple overlapping APs (WiFi jungle).

common_misconceptions.description: A BSS is the same as an ESS; in reality, an ESS consists of multiple BSSs connected via a distribution system.
A station must be in the same IP subnet as the AP to associate; association is at the link layer and independent of IP subnet.
A WiFi jungle always degrades performance; overlapping APs can be managed with proper channel planning and coordination.

children.title: 802.11 MAC Protocol (CSMA/CA)
children.summary: Explains the 802.11 medium access protocol, including CSMA/CA with random backoff, link-layer acknowledgments, and how it differs from Ethernet's CSMA/CD.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the 802.11 CSMA/CA protocol operation including channel sensing, DIFS, random backoff with binary exponential backoff, and link-layer acknowledgments.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners think CSMA/CA works like Ethernet's CSMA/CD with collision detection rather than collision avoidance.
Learners think the backoff counter decrements even when the channel is busy, instead of freezing during busy periods.
Learners think link-layer acknowledgments are optional in 802.11, when they are mandatory for unicast frames.
Learners think RTS/CTS is used for every frame transmission, while it is only used for larger frames or hidden terminal scenarios.

children.title: IEEE 802.11 Frame Format
children.summary: Describes the structure of 802.11 frames, including the address fields (which can differ from Ethernet addressing), frame types (data, control, management), and how frames are exchanged between a wireless host and an AP.
children.learning_objective: The learner can identify and explain the fields in an IEEE 802.11 frame, including the four address fields, payload, CRC, and frame control field, and describe how address fields are used for internetworking between wireless and wired networks.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners think 802.11 frames only need source and destination MAC addresses like Ethernet, overlooking the need for three or four address fields for internetworking.
Learners assume address 1, 2, 3, and 4 have fixed roles regardless of communication direction (e.g., from host to AP vs. AP to host).
Learners think the payload field is always 2,312 bytes rather than typically fewer than 1,500 bytes carrying an IP datagram or ARP packet.
Learners think the 32-bit CRC is optional because higher-layer protocols also provide error detection.

children.title: Mobility in the Same IP Subnet
children.summary: Examines how a wireless station hands over between access points within the same IP subnet, including association/reassociation and switch self-learning to keep the session intact.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how a wireless station maintains its IP address and ongoing TCP connections when moving between access points within the same IP subnet, including the role of switch self-learning and MAC address handling during handover.

common_misconceptions.description: The learner thinks the station must change its IP address when moving between APs in the same subnet.
The learner believes ongoing TCP connections are interrupted during intra-subnet handover.
The learner assumes a router is needed to interconnect APs for mobility within the same subnet.
The learner thinks switch self-learning cannot handle the MAC address changes during handover without MAC address spoofing.

children.title: Advanced 802.11 Features
children.summary: Covers advanced capabilities in 802.11 such as rate adaptation and power management, plus features like the WiFi Positioning System (WPS).
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how 802.11 rate adaptation and power management mechanisms improve wireless link reliability and device battery life.

common_misconceptions.description: Rate adaptation only changes the data rate without altering the underlying modulation and coding scheme.
Power management means the radio is completely turned off to save battery, rather than cycling between sleep and wake states.
WiFi Positioning System (WPS) is the same as Wi-Fi Protected Setup (also abbreviated WPS).
Every new 802.11 advanced feature requires brand new hardware rather than firmware or driver updates.

children.title: Bluetooth Personal Area Networks
children.summary: Introduces Bluetooth as a wireless personal area network technology, covering its architecture (piconets) and how it complements 802.11 WLANs.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe Bluetooth personal area network architecture including piconet master/client roles, time-division multiplexing, frequency hopping, and parked device power management.

common_misconceptions.description: Bluetooth is a wireless LAN technology like WiFi, but it is actually a wireless personal area network (WPAN) for short-range device connections.
Master and client devices have symmetric roles in a piconet, but the master controls the clock, frequency hopping, polling, and transmission power.
Bluetooth lacks power management features, but it supports parked devices that sleep and wake periodically to conserve energy.
Bluetooth operates on a fixed frequency, but it uses frequency-hopping spread spectrum across 79 channels.

children.title: Cellular Networks: 4G and 5G
children.summary: Cellular Internet access architecture: 4G LTE network elements and architecture, LTE protocol stacks and radio access network, network attachment and power management, the global cellular network as a network of networks, and emerging 5G cellular technology.

children.title: 4G LTE Architecture and Elements
children.summary: The 4G LTE network architecture and its key elements: base stations, the edge/core distinction, gateway and mobility-management components, and the separation of data and control planes.
children.learning_objective: The learner can identify and describe the key architectural elements of the 4G LTE network, including the radio access network, Enhanced Packet Core components (MME, S-GW, P-GW, HSS), and the separation of control and data planes.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners may think 4G LTE uses a circuit-switched core like 2G/3G, but it is an all-IP packet-switched architecture.
Learners may assume base stations connect directly to the Internet, but user traffic passes through the S-GW and P-GW in the EPC.
Learners may believe the MME processes user-plane data, but it is a control-plane entity only; the S-GW and P-GW handle user data.
Learners may overlook the explicit separation of control and data planes with logically centralized control in the LTE architecture.

children.title: LTE Protocol Stacks and Radio Access Network
children.summary: Protocol layering in LTE: the control-plane and data-plane protocol stacks and the radio access network connecting the mobile device to the base station.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the LTE user-plane protocol stack layers at the mobile node, base station, and serving gateway, and explain the role of the radio access network in connecting the mobile device to the base station.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners might think LTE introduces new transport-layer protocols, but it uses standard IP, TCP, and UDP.
Learners might confuse the Radio Access Network (base stations) with the core network (serving gateway, etc.).
Learners might think control-plane and user-plane protocol stacks are the same, but they differ in LTE.
Learners might expect detailed physical layer coverage, but the text notes physical layer details are left for another course.

children.title: LTE Network Attachment and Power Management
children.summary: How a mobile device attaches (registers) to an LTE network and the power-management techniques used to conserve device battery life.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the LTE network attachment process including synchronization signal detection, base station selection, and control-plane connection establishment.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners may think network attachment happens instantly, but it involves multiple synchronization and signaling steps.
Learners may assume a device can attach to any base station, but devices preferentially attach to their home network.
Learners may expect detailed power management techniques in this section, but the excerpts focus primarily on attachment.
Learners may think data plane is established first, but control-plane signaling connection is established first during attachment.

children.title: Global Cellular Network of Networks
children.summary: How a carrier's network interconnects with other carrier networks and the larger Internet to form a global cellular 'network of networks,' mirroring Internet architectural principles.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how cellular carrier networks interconnect with each other and the Internet to form a global 'network of networks,' identifying the role of gateway routers and IPX networks.

common_misconceptions.description: Cellular networks use fundamentally different architectural principles than the Internet.
Carriers interconnect exclusively through the public Internet rather than also using managed IPX networks.
The global cellular network is a single unified network rather than a network of independently operated carrier networks.
Interconnection between carriers only involves data-plane traffic, not control-plane signaling.

children.title: 5G Cellular Technology
children.summary: Emerging 5G cellular technology: new frequency bands (including millimeter-wave FR2), increased cell density, wider available spectrum, and MIMO/beam-forming for improved spectral efficiency.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain the key characteristics of 5G cellular technology including its frequency bands (FR1 and FR2), increased cell density due to millimeter-wave propagation, wider available spectrum, use of MIMO and beamforming for spectral efficiency, and core architecture changes such as control/user-plane separation.

common_misconceptions.description: 5G only uses millimeter-wave frequencies.
5G does not use MIMO technology.
5G core architecture is identical to 4G.
5G is only for fixed wireless Internet service.

children.title: Mobility Management: Principles
children.summary: The network-layer challenges of mobility: forms of device mobility, locating and routing to a mobile user, home networks versus roaming on visited networks, direct versus indirect routing, and handover as a user moves between points of attachment.

children.title: Device Mobility: A Network-Layer Perspective
children.summary: Introduces the spectrum of device mobility, from no mobility to mobility within the same IP subnet to full mobility across networks, and explains how each point on the spectrum poses different network-layer challenges for addressing, locating, and routing to a mobile user.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the spectrum of device mobility and explain the network-layer challenges (addressing, locating, routing) that arise at different points on this spectrum.

common_misconceptions.description: All mobility scenarios present the same network-layer challenges, but the spectrum from local to global mobility poses distinct challenges.
Direct routing to a mobile device is always feasible, but indirect routing via a home agent is often necessary when the device is in a visited network.
Mobile IP is obsolete, but its principles underlie modern 4G/5G mobility management.

children.title: Home Networks and Visited Networks
children.summary: Covers the roles of the home network as the central point of information and control for a mobile device, the visited (foreign) network that hosts the roaming device, and the control-plane functions (e.g., home agent, registration) used to track a device roaming among visited networks.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain the roles of home and visited networks in mobile roaming and describe the control-plane functions (HSS, home gateway) that track a mobile device's location across visited networks.

common_misconceptions.description: The Internet has a built-in concept of home and visited networks similar to cellular networks.
A mobile device always uses its permanent home IP address when attached to a visited network.
The home network gateway does not intercept datagrams destined for a roaming device.

children.title: Indirect Routing to a Mobile Device
children.summary: Explains the indirect (triangle) routing data-plane approach: a correspondent sends datagrams via the home network, which tunnels them to the mobile device's care-of address in the visited network, including how ongoing sessions are preserved as the device moves.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how indirect routing (triangle routing) forwards datagrams to a mobile device via its home network and a tunnel to the visited network, and how ongoing sessions are maintained during handover.

common_misconceptions.description: The learner thinks the correspondent directly addresses the mobile device's care-of address instead of its permanent address.
The learner believes indirect routing bypasses the home network, not realizing all datagrams traverse the home network first.
The learner assumes the tunnel endpoint between home and visited gateways remains fixed when the mobile device roams to a new visited network.
The learner thinks NAT translation is not needed at the visited gateway router for decapsulated datagrams.

children.title: Direct Routing to a Mobile Device
children.summary: Explains the direct routing data-plane approach: the correspondent learns the mobile device's current care-of address from the home network and then routes datagrams directly to the visited network, including the challenges of maintaining sessions during handover.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how direct routing works by describing the correspondent's query to the HSS to discover the visited network and subsequent direct tunneling of datagrams to the visited network gateway, and identify the two main challenges it introduces: the need for a mobile-user location protocol and the complexity of maintaining sessions during handover.

common_misconceptions.description: Direct routing still requires the home network HSS for the correspondent to discover the mobile device's current visited network.
When a mobile device moves to a new visited network, the correspondent does not automatically know the new location; additional mechanisms are needed to update the correspondent.
The correspondent does not send datagrams to the mobile device's permanent address directly; it uses the care-of address obtained from the HSS to tunnel datagrams to the visited network.

children.title: Handover Between Points of Attachment
children.summary: Covers the handover process by which a mobile device dynamically moves from one point of attachment to another, including the steps of breaking and establishing links, updating routing/addressing information, and who controls the handover (network vs. mobile device).
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the steps involved in handing over a mobile device from one base station to another, including the roles of the source and target base stations and the mobile device.

common_misconceptions.description: Handover is initiated solely by the mobile device, but actually the network (source and target base stations) controls the handover process.
The PDN gateway must be updated during every handover, but in local handovers within the same network the PDN gateway remains unaware.
Handover is complete once the mobile device switches to the target base station, but the source base station must still stop forwarding datagrams and perform cleanup.
Indirect routing through the home network is always used, but local breakout (tunneling to a visited network PDN gateway) is an alternative, though not widely deployed.

children.title: Impact of Wireless and Mobility on Higher Layers
children.summary: How wireless links and mobility affect transport- and application-layer protocols: TCP challenges over lossy wireless links, and treating bandwidth as a scarce commodity when serving content over cellular connections.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how wireless link characteristics and mobility affect TCP performance and why applications must treat bandwidth as a scarce resource over cellular networks.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners may think TCP interprets wireless packet loss as congestion, leading to unnecessary rate reduction.
Learners may assume wireless bandwidth is plentiful, ignoring scarcity in cellular networks.
Learners may believe mobility only impacts link-layer handover, not transport or application layers.
Learners may think there is a single standardized TCP variant for wireless, while research is ongoing.

children.title: What Is Network Security?
children.summary: Introduces the goals of secure communication (confidentiality, message integrity, end-point authentication, availability) and surveys prevalent Internet attacks: eavesdropping/sniffing, message modification, insertion, and deletion, impersonation, session hijacking, and denial of service.
children.learning_objective: The learner can define network security and list its four primary goals (confidentiality, message integrity, end-point authentication, availability) and describe common attack types (eavesdropping, message modification, impersonation, session hijacking, denial of service).

common_misconceptions.description: Network security is only about encryption, ignoring integrity, authentication, and availability.
A firewall alone provides complete network security.
Network attacks only come from external sources, not internal.
Network security can be made absolute rather than a risk management process.

children.title: Principles of Cryptography
children.summary: Fundamental cryptography techniques for encrypting communication, covering both symmetric key and public key encryption, which underpin all secure network protocols.

children.title: Symmetric Key Cryptography Basics
children.summary: The shared-secret-key model in which sender and receiver use the same key; classical ciphers such as the Caesar cipher; cryptanalysis approaches including brute-force and known-plaintext attacks.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the shared-secret-key model of symmetric key cryptography, explain the role of session keys, and identify common cryptanalysis approaches such as brute-force attacks.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners may think the same symmetric key is used for all communications rather than per-session keys.
Learners may assume symmetric key distribution is simple without a key distribution center or public-key assistance.
Learners may believe brute-force attacks are always practical against symmetric ciphers, ignoring large key spaces.
Learners may confuse symmetric key cryptography with public key cryptography, thinking they use the same key structure.

children.title: Block Ciphers and Stream Ciphers
children.summary: Modern symmetric techniques: block ciphers that encrypt fixed-size blocks (illustrated with a 3-bit example cipher, DES, and AES) and stream ciphers that encrypt bit by bit.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe how block ciphers encrypt fixed-size blocks using a key, and explain how Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode adds randomness to prevent identical plaintext blocks from producing identical ciphertext blocks.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners may think a small block size (e.g., 3 bits) provides sufficient security against brute-force attacks.
Learners may believe the initialization vector (IV) in CBC must be kept secret, whereas it is sent in the clear.
Learners may assume identical plaintext blocks always produce identical ciphertext blocks, not realizing CBC mode prevents this.
Learners may think brute-forcing a 56-bit DES key is infeasible, while NIST estimates it can be cracked with specialized hardware.

children.title: Cipher Block Chaining (CBC)
children.summary: Chaining ciphertext blocks together with an initialization vector (IV) so that identical plaintext blocks produce different ciphertext, avoiding the pattern leaks of encrypting blocks independently.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe how Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) uses an initialization vector (IV) and XOR chaining with the previous ciphertext block to ensure that identical plaintext blocks produce different ciphertext blocks.

common_misconceptions.description: The learner believes the IV must be kept secret like the key, but the excerpt states the IV is sent in the clear without compromising security.
