The learner thinks CBC guarantees all ciphertext blocks are unique, but the excerpt says identical plaintext blocks produce different ciphertexts 'almost always', not absolutely.
The learner assumes CBC adds significant bandwidth overhead, but the excerpt notes only one IV block is sent, negligibly increasing bandwidth.

children.title: Public Key Cryptography Concepts
children.summary: The two-key model with a publicly available key and a private key; how anyone can encrypt a message to a recipient while only the private-key holder can decrypt, and why a shared secret key implicitly identifies the sender while public key encryption does not.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the two-key model of public key cryptography, explain how public key encryption provides confidentiality, and contrast why shared secret keys implicitly identify the sender while public key encryption does not.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that encrypting a message with a recipient's public key automatically authenticates the sender, when in fact anyone can use the public key.
Thinking that the public key must be kept secret like a private key, whereas it is designed to be publicly available.
Assuming public key encryption is efficient for encrypting long messages directly, while it is typically used only to exchange a symmetric session key due to performance.

children.title: RSA Algorithm
children.summary: RSA key generation from primes p and q (computing n, z, choosing e and d), encryption and decryption via modular exponentiation, and why the algorithm works, with worked examples such as encrypting a word letter by letter.
children.learning_objective: The learner can describe the RSA key generation process, encryption and decryption operations, and explain why RSA works mathematically.

common_misconceptions.description: RSA typically encrypts a message block by block or uses hybrid encryption; encrypting a large message as a single integer is impractical.
RSA security relies on the difficulty of factoring large integers, which is not proven to be hard and may be broken by quantum computers.
The encryption exponent e and decryption exponent d are not interchangeable; e is typically small while d is large.
Generating large prime numbers for RSA requires probabilistic primality testing and is computationally intensive.

children.title: Message Integrity and Digital Signatures
children.summary: Techniques for detecting tampering of messages in transit: cryptographic hash functions, message authentication codes (MACs), and digital signatures.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how digital signatures use cryptographic hash functions and public-key cryptography to provide message integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation.

common_misconceptions.description: A cryptographic hash alone can ensure message integrity without a shared secret or digital signature.
MACs and digital signatures provide the same security properties and are interchangeable.
Digital signatures encrypt the entire message for confidentiality rather than signing a hash of the message.
The private key is used to encrypt the message content when creating a digital signature.

children.title: End-Point Authentication
children.summary: Protocols for verifying the identity of the party with whom one is communicating, using nonces and shared secrets to defeat replay and impersonation attacks.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain the purpose of end-point authentication and describe how nonces and shared secrets are used to prevent replay and impersonation attacks.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that verifying the source IP address alone is sufficient for end-point authentication.
Assuming that reusing nonces does not weaken authentication against replay attacks.
Thinking that using public key cryptography without certificates prevents man-in-the-middle attacks.

children.title: Securing E-Mail
children.summary: Application-layer security for e-mail (e.g., PGP), combining digital signatures with symmetric and public key encryption to secure the e-mail message chain.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how PGP combines symmetric encryption, public-key encryption, and digital signatures to provide confidentiality, sender authentication, and message integrity for e-mail.

common_misconceptions.description: Learners may think symmetric key distribution is easy, but it requires a secure channel.
Learners may assume public-key encryption is efficient for long messages, but it is slow; hybrid encryption with session keys is used.
Learners may confuse digital signatures with encryption, but signatures provide authentication and integrity, not confidentiality.
Learners may think public keys are automatically trusted, but distribution and verification (e.g., via certificates) is a nontrivial problem.

children.title: Securing TCP Connections: TLS
children.summary: Transport-layer security for TCP connections, covering how TLS provides encryption, message integrity, and end-point authentication, including handshaking and the record protocol.
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how TLS secures TCP connections by describing its position in the protocol stack, the three phases of the TLS handshake (handshake, key derivation, data transfer), and the services it provides (encryption, integrity, authentication).

common_misconceptions.description: TLS is a separate protocol layer above TCP rather than a sublayer between the application and TCP.
The TLS handshake occurs before the TCP connection is established.
TLS provides only encryption and not message integrity or endpoint authentication.
TLS encrypts data at the application layer instead of between the application and TCP socket.

children.title: Network-Layer Security: IPsec and VPNs
children.summary: Blanket protection at the network layer using the IPsec protocol suite, and its application in building virtual private networks (VPNs).
children.learning_objective: The learner can explain how IPsec provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication at the network layer and how it is used to construct virtual private networks (VPNs) over the public Internet.

common_misconceptions.description: IPsec only operates between end hosts, not between routers or other network-layer entities.
IPsec always encrypts the entire original IP packet, including the original IP header.
IPsec is a single protocol rather than a suite of protocols (AH, ESP, IKE, etc.).
A VPN built with IPsec requires dedicated physical circuits instead of running over the public Internet.
